10251-town-geology:
These Victorian lectures explain geology for town readers who may never visit a quarry or a cliff. The writer starts with the soil under a field, then builds outward to rocks, strata, and the long ages that shaped them. His image is simple: geology studies the rind of the earth, while astronomy asks what lies inside.

Later talks show how hills, valleys, coasts, and city ground were made and worn away. The style is friendly and full of homely comparisons, aimed at curious minds rather than experts. Readers get a clear, old-style introduction to how the ground beneath a town came to be.
13205-civics-as-applied-sociology:
Patrick Geddes's Civics as Applied Sociology, read before the Sociological Society on July 18, 1904, with Charles Booth in the chair, argues that cities must be surveyed before they can be governed. Geddes begins with London, vast and foggy, and asks where a civic survey should start. He praises Booth's social survey, yet notes even London remains a labyrinth.

Geddes holds that civics is the joint life of a city, too much for one man to hold, and that each town must work out its own scheme. He cites Rowntree's work in York, done with his advice, as a model of local study. Tradition, he adds, is to a community what memory is to a person. The paper is a founding text of town planning as social science.
15076-some-principles-of-maritime-strate:
Julian S. Corbett's 1911 work Some Principles of Maritime Strategy sets out theory of war, natures of wars offensive and defensive, limited and unlimited, limited war and maritime empires, and wars of intervention. Conditions of strength in limited war follow.

Theory of the object, command of the sea, theory of means, constitution of fleets, and theory of method, concentration and dispersal of force, complete the first part. Methods of securing, disputing and exercising command follow. Corbett writes for naval officers and students, arguing sea power is about command, not merely battle. The book shaped British naval thought before the First World War.
15120-the-broadway-anthology:
Four New York writers of 1917 join forces in this anthology of Broadway life, with Edward Bernays, Samuel Hoffenstein, Walter Kingsley, and Murdock Pemberton each taking a section. Poems and short prose pieces cover press agents, chorus men, prima donnas, and first nights. The book first ran in New York papers and magazines.

Bernays writes of accidents, photographs, and the distribution of credit, while Hoffenstein turns to scrubwomen, jesters, and cabaret singers. Kingsley sketches George M. Cohan and David Belasco, and Pemberton closes with Pavlova and night-time Broadway. Together they give a lively, insider portrait of the stage world just before America entered the war.
16136-american-addresses-with-a-lecture-:
Thomas H. Huxley's American Addresses, published in London by Macmillan in 1877, gathers his 1876 visit to the United States. Three New York lectures on evolution open the book, testing the hypotheses of nature's history, the neutral and favorable evidence, and the demonstrative evidence for evolution. An address at the opening of Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore follows, with a lecture on studying biology at South Kensington.

Huxley, Darwin's great defender, argues with clarity, wit, and a teacher's patience. The volume shows Victorian science speaking to a new American audience at a hopeful moment. Students of evolution, education, and science writing will find it a landmark collection.
1656-apology:
In Athens in 399 BC, an old man stood before a jury of his fellow citizens. He faced two charges: that he did not believe in the city's gods, and that he corrupted the young. Charged with impiety and with corrupting the young, Socrates answers by describing his life. He cites the oracle's claim that no man was wiser, his habit of questioning statesmen, poets, and craftsmen, and his refusal to flatter the jury.

The speech ends with his conviction and death sentence, and with Socrates still insisting that a good man cannot be harmed by an unjust verdict. Readers meet the philosopher at his most direct, arguing that knowing one's ignorance is worth more than reputation, and that he would rather die than stop asking questions.
17229-the-haunted-hour-an-anthology:
Margaret Widdemer's 1920 anthology, The Haunted Hour, gathers poems of ghosts, All Souls, and the night between saints and souls. Contents run from Katherine Tynan's All-Souls and Lizette Reese's All-Saints' Eve to George Macdonald's Janet's Tryst, Marjorie Pickthall's Mary Shepherdess, and Yeats's folk of the air. Permissions from Doran, Dutton, Harper, Holt, and Macmillan fill the copyright page.

Widdemer groups poems by mood: sighing souls, little dead children, and purgatory's open door. The set suits readers who like ghost verse that is tender as well as eerie. It is a fine Halloween shelf book, where classic and modern poets meet in the haunted hour.
17280-anthropology:
R. R. Marett's Anthropology, number 37 in the Home University Library, surveys the science of man in ten chapters. Scope, antiquity of man, race, environment, language, social organization, law, religion, morality, and man the individual run from page 7 to 241, with a bibliography and index. Marett, reader in social anthropology at Oxford, opens with prehistoric brothers born and died in darkness, yet rescuing the torch of life for us.

His prose is clear, humane, and general, made for readers new to the field. The book suits students who want a short, classic map of anthropology's questions. As a period survey, it shows early twentieth-century science at work, and should be read with its age in mind.
18188-homer-and-classical-philology:
Friedrich Nietzsche gave Homer and Classical Philology as his inaugural address at Basel University on May 28, 1869, printed here from his collected works, translated by J. M. Kennedy. Nietzsche, then a young professor, asks what classical philology truly is.

He finds no clear, agreed view of the field, since it mixes history, science, and art under one name, like a magic potion of odd liquors, ores, and bones. Yet it holds an artistic, moral force that lifts it past mere learning. The address is short, bold, and early Nietzsche, a fine start for readers who want his mind before the great books.
18911-biology:
Edmund Beecher Wilson, professor of zoology at Columbia, delivered this lecture on biology at the university on November 20, 1907, published by the Columbia University Press in 1908. Wilson warns at the outset that no single science owns the name biology, which covers a whole group of sciences of life.

The biologist's double task, he says, is to resolve the living organism into simpler factors, through morphology and physiology, and to study it as a product of history. Darwin, more than any other, brought home that present life is the outcome of evolution, and that morphology and physiology are inseparable. The lecture serves as a preface to fuller talks on physiology, botany, and zoology.
19019-aids-to-forensic-medicine-and-toxi:
W. G. Aitchison Robertson, a lecturer in Edinburgh, wrote this 1922 handbook of forensic medicine and toxicology in its ninth edition. It guides doctors who must give evidence, examine the dead, and judge sudden death, poisoning, and crime. The book is meant for students and working practitioners alike.

Chapters cover personal identity, signs of death, coroners' inquests, and the care a medical witness must take with his sworn words. Fees, statutes, and court practice are set out in plain terms. Readers get a clear, practical aid to law and medicine, firm on duty and detail.
19499-music-notation-and-terminology:
Karl W. Gehrkens wrote this guide to music notation and terms, published in the mid nineteen teens. Chapters define symbols, abbreviations, signs, and embellishments, then move through scales, measure, tempo, and the words that tell players how a piece should sound.

A section on recitative explains speech-like song, once backed by a single cello line, with full chords shown only by signs and figures. The book, with audio in its online form, remains a clear primer for students learning to read music. A chapter on embellishments teaches the trill, the mordent, and the turn, each with its own sign.
19518-siouan-sociology:
James Owen Dorsey wrote this posthumous paper on Siouan sociology, printed in the Smithsonian's annual report for the mid eighteen nineties. Dorsey, sent to Dakota as a missionary in his early twenties, won Native trust by his ear for language and spent two years learning Ponka and kindred dialects.

The paper maps tribal groups, from the Kwapa villages known to French explorers to clans named for taboos such as not touching a buffalo calf. It remains a careful record of Siouan kinship and social order, built on fieldwork rather than guesswork.
21099-more-about-peggy:
Mrs G. de Horne Vaizey continues the story of Peggy in this sequel from the end of the nineteenth century. Its world already has electricity, telephones, trains, and buses, though middle-class homes still run on servants. The book opens at sea, on a P and O steamer crossing the Bay of Bengal toward England in bright sun.

Peggy's feelings and friendships carry the story more than big events do. Vaizey was known for girls' fiction that took young women's inner lives seriously. Snow in England waits at the end of the voyage home. Readers of the first Peggy book get the same warm, observant manner here.
22668-poems-of-to-day-an-anthology:
Poems of To-Day is an anthology of modern English verse, gathered for schools and general readers in the years of the Great War. The catalog record names no editor and gives no year. Its preface explains the plan: a gathering meant to show what living poets made of history, faith, and daily duty.

The poems fall into three groups, the editor says, beginning with poems of history and of England's own tradition and the duties that tradition lays on its heirs. Some poems come straight from the present war, yet the editor hopes nothing here will shame the book in happier days. Such anthologies carried new poets into classrooms by the thousand. This one preserves the taste of its moment: earnest, patriotic, and hungry for beauty under fire.
22748-explanation-of-terms-used-in-entom:
Explanation of Terms Used in Entomology is a glossary of the technical language of insect science, prepared for an entomological society's new edition. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Every science builds a vocabulary of hard words, and entomology's, drawn from Latin and Greek, needed a standard key.

The preface tells how the work grew: the society voted for a new edition and gave the writer two associates to prepare it. They expected a light summer job of dropping obsolete terms and adding a few new ones, with a report due in fall. It proved larger, as glossaries do. The book still serves historians of science, and any reader who has wondered what entomologists mean by their harder words.
2378-select-epigrams-from-the-greek-anth:
J. W. Mackail selects epigrams from the Greek Anthology, the great collection of short poems spanning the ancient world. Select Epigrams offers love poems, epitaphs, dedications, and jokes, translated with grace and brevity. Mackail's choices favor wit and feeling over obscurity, making the ancient voices feel near.

The epigrams range from tender to biting, often within a few lines. The volume serves as an ideal introduction to Greek lyric in miniature. Poetry lovers will find a book to dip into again and again. Mackail also translated Virgil and wrote a life of William Morris.
24456-fathers-of-biology:
Charles McRae, formerly a scholar of Exeter College, Oxford, published this book in London in 1890. It tells the lives of five great naturalists. Each one, McRae argues, pushed biology forward in a distinct way. The book aims to show students that the facts of anatomy and physiology were not all found by recent workers.

Through biography, McRae traces how each naturalist observed, experimented, and reasoned. Their work built the knowledge later generations took for granted. The book suits readers who want the human story behind biology: curious, hard-working observers whose discoveries still shape how the science is taught.
25448-peggy:
Laura E. Richards writes of New England village life in this story of Peggy and her circle. A Boston Post notice praises her delicate treatment of village character, and the front matter recalls Captain January and Melody. The tale follows young people through courtship, weddings, and family feeling, with humour and warmth.

Its wedding scene comes through Gertrude's eager retelling, as Roger and his bride speak clearly at the altar and the music breaks out. Jerry and the colonel nearly break down, and the colonel's nose-blowing makes Jerry wince. Gertrude, once nicknamed Chelsea Waterworks for her tears, has nearly outgrown her childish weeping. The book belongs to Richards' Margaret books.
25601-fasting-girls-their-physiology-and:
William A. Hammond, professor of diseases of the mind and nervous system in New York and Vermont, writes this 1879 study of fasting girls, published by Putnam. His epigraphs borrow Ecclesiastes, that there is no new thing under the sun, and Phaedrus, urging ears neither to scorn nor to trust at once.

Hammond, also author of a book on cerebral hyperaemia from mental strain, examines girls famed for living without food, testing claims against physiology and pathology. The study asks what the body can bear, what illness or fraud may explain, and how doctors should judge wonders that draw crowds.
26382-ancient-america-in-notes-on-americ:
John D. Baldwin's Ancient America, issued by Harper and Brothers in 1871, sums up what was then known of American antiquities. Baldwin, author of Pre-Historic Nations, notes that knowledge lay scattered in French, Spanish, and great English quartos, with no single work giving a whole view. His book aims to fill that gap for general readers, covering all time before Columbus.

A gateway at Labna fronts the volume, and later pages follow Lieutenant Whipple west along the thirty-fifth parallel. Ruins show cedar beams, obsidian arrow heads, and painted pottery, with a Pueblo ruin at Pecos among the sights. A paper on Pacific Island antiquities closes the set. The book offers a Victorian survey of mounds, cities, and relics across the Americas.
27500-the-new-theology:
R. J. Campbell, minister of the City Temple in London, published this statement of liberal theology with the Macmillan Company in New York in March 1907, reprinted the next month. Campbell begins by separating religion from theology: religion and theology differ: theology gives intellectual form to religious experience, and no one with a real religious experience can help having one.

Chapters take up God and the universe, man in relation to God, the nature of evil, and the eternal Christ. They go on to the incarnation and the atonement in three parts, covering its association with Jesus, Semitic ideas of atonement, and its place in Christian history and experience. Scripture, salvation and judgment, and the church and kingdom close the book. It stirred wide debate in its day.
27842-the-economic-aspect-of-geology:
C. K. Leith of the University of Wisconsin wrote this 1921 textbook on the economic aspects of geology, published by Henry Holt and Company. It surveys how each branch of geology bears on finding and using mineral deposits.

Chapters cover the common elements, minerals, and rocks of the earth, the classification of deposits, and their formation by igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic processes. Leith wrote for students and prospectors who needed geology as a practical science, linking field observation to mines, ores, and industry. Leith surveys mineralogy, stratigraphy, structural geology, physiography, and metamorphism in his opening chapter.
28496-introduction-to-the-science-of-soc:
Robert E. Park and Ernest W. Burgess prepared Introduction to the Science of Sociology for the University of Chicago Press, published in September 1921. The volume gathers readings from many writers, with Thorndike, Shinn, Moll, and Myers among those quoted on human nature. Each chapter pairs source passages with topics for written themes and questions for discussion.

Chapters move from sociology and the social sciences through human nature, society and the group, and isolation. They then treat social contacts, interaction, forces, competition, conflict, and accommodation. Students get a structured survey of early sociology, built from original texts rather than summary alone.
29125-brief-reflections-relative-to-the-:
The author of Evelina and Cecilia, Frances Burney, wrote this pamphlet in London in 1793, priced at one shilling and sixpence. Its profits went wholly to the relief of the emigrant French clergy, priests who had fled revolutionary France for Britain. Burney addresses her reflections earnestly to the humane consideration of the ladies of Great Britain.

Burney apologizes for a woman entering public matters, then argues that women are not mere passive spectators of moral and political life. Their duties, she says, bind them to help the suffering. Readers get a short, urgent charity appeal from the French Revolution's shadow, and a glimpse of how a famous novelist argued for women's public compassion.
29234-presentation-pieces-in-the-museum-:
Margaret Brown Klapthor wrote this study, paper 47 from the Museum of History and Technology, on presentation pieces in the museum's collection. Presentation pieces are objects given to honor a person: swords, snuffboxes, ships in miniature, and more, from the eighteenth, nineteenth, and twentieth centuries.

Klapthor groups them by occasion: service in the War of 1812, peace and friendship, politics, the Mexican, Civil, and Indian wars, and service in the Spanish-American War and World War I. There are pieces for Mary Todd Lincoln, for engineering, diplomacy, Arctic exploration, suffragettes, sports, and trowels for cornerstone layings and fire trumpets. Readers get a museum catalogue that doubles as a history of American honor, gift by gift.
2935-on-the-study-of-zoology:
Thomas Henry Huxley wrote On the Study of Zoology as a defense of natural history, the study of minerals, plants, and animals. He recalls Linnaeus as a naturalist in the wide sense, whose Systema Naturae gathered all that was known of natural bodies in his time. The essay distinguishes the natural sciences from other physical sciences and explains what a naturalist actually does. Huxley brings a lobster to life as his example.

He imagines a reader who knows it only as an inert mass, an organic crystal, and then sees it tear and crush flesh with multitudinous jaws. The new question becomes how all this takes place, and the new idea is adaptation to a way of life. The essay still serves as an invitation to zoology for curious beginners.
29622-the-book-of-common-prayer-and-the-:
Printed in Edinburgh by Cambridge University Press and approved in November 1912 by the Primus of the Scottish Episcopal Church, this volume joins the Book of Common Prayer to the Scottish Liturgy. It holds the administration of sacraments and other rites of the Church of England. The Psalter stands pointed as psalms are to be sung or said in churches, with forms for making bishops, priests, and deacons.

Its contents run from morning and evening prayer through the Creed of St. Athanasius, the Litany, and prayers and thanksgivings for the whole year, with permitted additions and changes for the Scottish Church. Readers of liturgy will find a complete, historic service book for worship in the Anglican tradition.
30219-monophysitism-past-and-present-a-s:
A. A. Luce, fellow of Trinity College, Dublin, and late captain of the 12th Royal Irish Rifles, studies Monophysitism past and present as a question in Christology. The Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge published the London volume in 1920, with Macmillan in New York, printed by Clowes in London and Beccles. Chapters treat the metaphysical basis of Monophysitism, its origins, its doctrine, its ethos, its relation to modern psychology, and its present day.

Luce opens by calling Monophysitism a Christological heresy of the fifth century, the church condemned it at the mid-century Council of Chalcedon. It survived condemnation to flourish in the East for several centuries, and its adherents formed themselves into lasting bodies. Books consulted range from Assemani and Harnack to Robertson, Windelband, Wright, and Bergson, giving the essay a scholarly frame.
30276-some-imagist-poets-an-anthology:
Some Imagist Poets gathers six poets in an anthology published by Houghton Mifflin in April 1915, from the Riverside Press at Cambridge. Richard Aldington opens with childhood, the poplar, Round-Pond, daisy, epigrams, and a faun seeing snow for the first time. The pool, the garden, sea lily, sea iris, sea rose, Oread, and Orion dead show the short, hard images the school prized, in poems signed H. D.

John Gould Fletcher adds the blue symphony and a London excursion, while F. S. Flint offers trees, lunch, malady, accident, and houses. D. H. Lawrence contributes a ballad of another Ophelia, fireflies in the corn, the mowers, and scent of irises. Amy Lowell closes with Venus transiens, the travelling bear, the letter, grotesque, and the bombardment, plus a bibliography and thanks to four magazines.
31382-psychology:
Robert S. Woodworth's Psychology: A Study of Mental Life, published by Henry Holt in New York in 1921, was the standard American textbook of its generation. Woodworth, professor of psychology at Columbia University, opens by asking what psychology is and does. He treats it as both a science of consciousness and a science of behavior, using introspection and objective observation.

Later chapters take up reactions and reaction time, reflex action, nerves and nerve centers, the synapse and coordination, reactions of different levels, and motor centers lower and higher. They go on to how the brain produces muscular movement, facilitation and inhibition, and the speech, auditory, visual, and other sensory centers, with the cerebellum. Each chapter ends with exercises and references, making the book a complete course in the psychology of its day.
31754-devil-stories-an-anthology:
Maximilian J. Rudwin's 1921 anthology Devil Stories, selected and edited with introduction and critical comments and published by Alfred A. Knopf, opens with Heine's warning that the fire everlasting is no idle fairy tale. Rudwin planned a whole series of diabolical literature, including devil plays, essays, legends, and an anthology of Satanic verse.

The volume's discussions range from Baudelaire's preface to The Flowers of Evil, where ennui appears as the most foul vice of all. They reach Gorky's story The Devil, in which the devil himself suffers from ennui. Readers get a literary tour of the devil in story, from temptation and bargains to boredom itself.
32819-elegy:
Charles Beaumont tells of a lost ship and an impossible city, in this story from Imagination Stories of Science and Fantasy of February 1953. Captain Webber's vessel had nearly exhausted its fuel months after leaving Earth, and the crew knows they are lost.

Then Mr. Friden, looking through a screen for something to do, reports houses on an asteroid where no asteroid should be. Webber lands his men and finds a city of still, stationary people. A pamphlet on a stool names the place: Happy Glades, beneath a photograph of a white cherub on a granite slab. The city keeps its secret until the last page.
33485-village-life-in-china-a-study-in-s:
Arthur H. Smith's Village Life in China, a study in sociology published in 1899, draws on twenty-six years as a missionary of the American Board in China. Smith, with sixteen illustrations from photographs, an index, and a glossary, writes of village ways without glamour, yet with respect for qualities that made the people enduring. His book was praised for its honest, humane view.

The study's value lies in its close, lived detail on family, work, faith, and custom in rural China. Its tone is earnest and observant, aimed at readers who want China as it was, not as romance painted it. For students of Chinese history, it remains a classic, if dated, portrait of village life before great change.
3374-the-entire-march-family-trilogy:
William Dean Howells's March family trilogy gathers three novels in one volume. Their Wedding Journey leads, from the outset through a midsummer-day's dream, the night boat, and a day's railroading. The enchanted city and beyond, Niagara, down the St Lawrence, and the sentiment of Montreal follow, with homeward and home, Niagara revisited, and twelve years after their wedding.

A Hazard of New Fortunes, in five parts, forms the middle panel, and Their Silver Wedding Journey, in three volumes, closes the set. Together the three books follow Basil and Isabel March from honeymoon to silver wedding, across a changing America. Readers get Howells's great domestic chronicle whole: one marriage, three journeys, and a nation's manners in between.
34279-handbook-of-medical-entomology:
Handbook of Medical Entomology, printed at Ithaca in 1915, was written by Riley and Johannsen, two professors at Cornell. Riley taught insect form and the study of parasites, and Johannsen taught biology. Their book treats the branch of insect study that bears on human health and disease.

The first chapter asks how insects spread disease and how jointed animals can harm man. Later parts take up spiders, scorpions, mites, ticks, and biting insects that are directly poisonous. Long lists of corrections and fine drawings show a working science text, made for students and health staff who needed to name the pests they met.
34502-charles-lyell-and-modern-geology:
Bonney wrote Charles Lyell and Modern Geology for the Century Science Series, edited by Roscoe. Macmillan issued the New York printing in 1895 alongside Cassell in London. The preface owns that Lyell's life lacks flood, field, and danger for spice. No brigand, beast, or hard block troubled his smooth, well aided career in life.

Yet Bonney finds a lesson worth the telling in that quiet record in full. Young Lyell vowed to set geology, then barely a science, on sounder ground at once. Years of travel, watching, and exact writing trained him for the Principles of Geology. Labour, money, and fatigue were spent without grudge toward that single goal in sight. A science grows up inside one patient life.
35001-friction-lubrication-and-the-lubri:
Lewis, president of the Philadelphia Horological Society, wrote Friction, Lubrication and the Lubricants in Horology, published by Hazlitt at Chicago in 1896 with half-tones and drawings by the author. Five chapters move from the sources and refinement of watch oils, through the physics of friction, to its laws applied in horology and the relative values of lubricants. The introduction argues that all the science of escapements, adjusting, and factory machinery is wasted if the maker or repairer neglects the oil.

Watches excellent in every other respect, Lewis says, come to untimely ends because their construction fails to keep oil where it is needed. A repairer may clean and restore a piece perfectly, yet its rate fails within the year from bad oil or bad oiling. The book gathers the profession's literature in concise form for working watchmakers. Lewis illustrates the mechanisms himself.
35317-geology:
Geology, an elementary manual by James Geikie of the Geological Survey, was issued by Chambers in 1883. The book belongs to the Chambers Elementary Science Manuals. Geikie had written The Great Ice Age before this primer. Chambers of London and Edinburgh published the series for all classes.

The preface tells why such manuals were put into print. The vital importance of spreading some knowledge of science is daily more felt, it says. Chambers resolved to meet and promote that movement with cheap manuals. A primer of geology teaches rocks, fossils, and the shaping of the earth. Geikie writes plainly, from his survey field work in Scotland. The small book put the new science into working men’s hands.
35354-moral-theology:
John A McHugh and Charles J Callan present Moral Theology, a complete course based on St Thomas Aquinas and the best modern authorities, from Joseph F Wagner of New York. Edward P Farrell revised and enlarged it, and the imprimatur of Cardinal Spellman is dated May 24, 1958. The revisor's note calls it a revision, not a rewriting, of a manual standard for thirty years.

The contents open with the definition, objects, sources, and methods of moral theology, then turn to general moral theology. The last end of man, acts as human, moral, and meritorious, the passions, and good and bad habits fill the design.
35470-key-to-the-science-of-theology:
Key to the Science of Theology is a religious treatise by Parley P Pratt, published at Liverpool and in London in 1855. The London seller was the Saints' Book Depot in Jewin Street. Pratt offers the book as an introduction to the first principles of spiritual philosophy, religion, law, and government.

His contents range wide. Ancient American records stand near the front. Keys of the mysteries of the Godhead come next, then the origin and destiny of the universe. A key of knowledge, power, and government follows. The philosophy of miracles, angels and spirits, and dreams each get a chapter. The world of spirits and the resurrection lead to the three heavens: Telestial, Terrestrial, and Celestial. Laws of marriage and procreation close the list. Pratt presents the system as truth delivered by the ancients and restored in his own age.
37411-a-primer-of-assyriology:
A H Sayce, professor of Assyriology at Oxford, wrote a Primer of Assyriology, first issued in September eighteen ninety-four. The small book carried seven pictures, among them a clay cylinder of Tiglath-Pileser the First. Sayce had written other works on the ancient East.

The primer starts with the land and peoples of Babylonia and Assyria. It then tells how the carved records were found and read, and how the reading was tested. A long chapter gives the history of the two lands, from the first empire to the fall of Babylon. Faith, gods such as Istar, priests, temples, and views of the next life follow.
37469-some-imagist-poets-1916-an-annual-:
The annual anthology for 1916, issued by Houghton Mifflin in Boston and New York in the New Poetry Series, gathers six imagist poets. Richard Aldington, the poet who signs H D, John Gould Fletcher, Flint, Lawrence, and Amy Lowell each contribute a group of poems. A bibliography closes the volume.

The poets thank the editors of The Egoist, Poetry and Drama, The Little Review, and Poetry of Chicago, whose editor, Harriet Monroe, is credited with introducing imagism to the world. Aldington opens with Eros and Psyche, set by a grimy statue in a Camden Town yard. Lowell's group includes Patterns and her Stravinsky piece for string quartet.
37488-asgard-stories-tales-from-norse-my:
Mary Foster and Mabel Cummings retold tales from Norse myth for young readers in a book dated 1901. They had told the tales in class for years and shaped them here for school and home use. Odin, named the Allfather, stands at the head of the gods of Asgard in their telling.

The preface argues that tales of the North should come before tales of Greece for young pupils. Cold lands, hard work, and a stern sense of right and wrong fill the old stories. Short forms, clear words, and a guide to names at the back help new readers keep the gods and places straight.
3772-the-student-s-elements-of-geology:
Charles Lyell, author of the Principles of Geology, abridged his great work into this student textbook, rich with more than six hundred woodcut illustrations. The book sorts rocks by origin and age, from aqueous strata laid down in water to volcanic, plutonic, and metamorphic forms, and it explains stratification, fossils, and the earth's crust in order. Tertiary, Secondary, and Primary divisions frame the whole story of deep time.

Later chapters read fossils as evidence, with corals, shells, crocodile teeth, and a thirteen foot sea snake from Sheppey pointing to vanished shores. Lyell writes with the calm authority that made him the age's chief geologist. Students of earth science history will find a clear window on Victorian geology, while general readers gain a solid first map of rocks and ages.
37741-kankanay-ceremonies-american-archa:
C R Moss published Kankanay Ceremonies in 1920 as a University of California paper in American archaeology and ethnology, running some forty pages. The Kankanay are a people of the northern Philippines. Contents open with comparative culture and the ceremonial system, compared with the neighbouring Nabaloi.

Sections treat spirits and deities, priesthood, divination, spoken ritual, dancing and songs, and omens and taboo. Long lists name particular ceremonies of the Lepanto Kankanay, north and south. Myths close the paper, covering the origin of thunder, of lightning, and of man, and the mountain Kabunian. Readers get an early ethnographic record of Igorot ritual life.
40404-the-elements-of-geology:
The Elements of Geology is a textbook by Norton, professor of geology at Cornell College in Iowa, published by Ginn in 1905. An introductory note by Davis of Harvard explains the plan the two men worked out by correspondence. The needs of the young student, not the expert, set the book's scope.

The arrangement is twofold. The principles of physical geology come first, in a natural order suited to most of the country. The historical view follows, setting the same processes into the story of the earth and its succession of inhabitants, with special attention to North America. Davis insists that a textbook is only one factor in good teaching beside the teacher, the laboratory and the local field. The method is inductive throughout: the student is shown the evidence that leads to each conclusion, not merely handed the conclusions of authorities.
40606-the-legal-position-of-the-clergy:
P V Smith, chancellor of the Manchester diocese, wrote a handbook on the legal place of the clergy, printed in London in 1905. The book sits in a series of handbooks for clergy edited by Arthur Robinson, vicar of a London church by the Tower. Smith had earlier written on the law of churchwardens.

Chapter one maps the ground, from the standing of clergy in church and civil law to the sources of church law. Old canons, acts of Parliament, and church court rulings all count as sources. Later heads cover patrons and the right to name a rector, new parishes, bishops, archdeacons, and rural deans.
41283-the-heroes-of-asgard-tales-from-sc:
The Heroes of Asgard retells tales from Scandinavian mythology, by the Keary authors, with illustrations by Huard. Macmillan printed it in New York in 1909, a reprint of the revised edition of 1906. A preface explains that the revisers cut the conversations framing each chapter, corrected inaccuracies, and added fresh information from sources not consulted at first, naming Simrock, Mallet, Laing, Thorpe, Howitt, and Dasent.

An introduction on the religion of the ancient Scandinavians precedes nine chapters of myth. The Aesir come first, with the children of Loki and the bridge Bifrost. Thor's journey to Jotunheim follows, then Frey and fairest Gerd, the wanderings of Freyja, and Iduna's apples. Baldur's dream and death form the sixth chapter. The binding of Fenrir, the punishment of Loki, and Ragnarok, the twilight of the gods, close the book, with an index of names and meanings at the end.
41351-practical-exercises-in-elementary-:
Practical Exercises in Elementary Meteorology is a laboratory manual by Robert DeCourcy Ward, instructor in climatology at Harvard University. It was printed at Boston in 1899. In his preface Ward says the growth of weather study as a school subject has been held back by the lack of a printed outline of work for the school years.

Good text-books exist for advanced study, he notes, but no laboratory manual serves the first steps of the science. In many schools the scholars already keep weather records, yet with little system and little clear result. Ward's book gives a guide to simple observation and reasoning from what is seen. It is not meant to replace the text-books. The facts found through the exercises are left for the newer text-books to explain. The manual builds a foundation on which later studies may rest.
41892-dynamic-thought-or-the-law-of-vibr:
William Walker Atkinson sets out his law of energy in Dynamic Thought, issued in 1906 by the Segnogram Publishing Company of Los Angeles. Atkinson had edited New Thought and co-edited The Segnogram, and he presents the book as a marriage of ancient occult teaching to the latest ideas of modern science. A Galvini saying about his two sets of critics stands at the front as a motto.

The foreword argues that occultists reach facts first but prove them badly, while science denies those facts until they are thrust under its eyes. Once forced to accept them, science builds better proofs and claims the result as its own discovery, a bargain Atkinson means to hold both sides to here.
4204-the-elements-of-geology:
W. H. Norton's Elements of Geology explains the earth for students, chapter by chapter, from rain to rock. A chapter on rivers and valleys turns from water that soaks into the ground to the run-off that washes along the surface.

Fed by rains and melting snows, the run-off gathers into faint courses that join deeper channels, as twigs join stems. In humid climates, larger ravines carry the flow onward, cutting valleys as they go. Readers who want geology in plain, patient prose will find a clear textbook of land and water.
42055-your-mind-and-how-to-use-it-a-manu:
William Walker Atkinson wrote a manual of working psychology in 1911. He holds that a sound mind is not enough unless its owner learns how to use it well. Early chapters ask what the mind is, how states of mind work, and what the great nerve centres do, before reaching the waking self and its powers.

Long parts treat notice, sight, memory, fancy, and the whole range of feelings, from the brute urges and passions to social, church and art loves. Later chapters take up thought itself, the making of ideas, judgment, sound and false reasoning, and end with the will, its training, and a tonic for weak resolve.
42508-curious-creatures-in-zoology:
John Ashton's Curious Creatures in Zoology, with 130 illustrations throughout the text, was published by Nimmo in 1890. A publisher's note limits the edition: two hundred and ten copies printed on superfine Royal octavo paper, each numbered, the type distributed after. This copy is number 175.

Ashton's preface states his rescue work. Travellers see strange things, he begins, especially when their writing is not put under the microscope of modern science. Our ancestors, a stay-at-home race, could not confute the stories they read, and that age of faith had its comforts. Now they are falling into oblivion, and Ashton compiles this book to save some of them. He lets the old authors tell their stories in their own old-fashioned language rather than paraphrase, with reproductions of the quaint wood engravings. The greatest wonders, he notes, have been met with in the sea, above all in the Northern Ocean.
42626-careers-in-atomic-energy:
Careers in Atomic Energy is a guidance booklet by McIlhenny for students. The Atomic Energy Commission issued it in its Understanding the Atom series. A foreword says nuclear energy touches every American man, woman, and child. It will affect all peoples of the earth in years ahead. Brunenkant, director of technical information, signs that foreword for the commission.

Seaborg chaired the commission in the front matter of this booklet. Ramey, Johnson, Thompson, and Larson served as members beside him there. Contents open with the scientific mind and scientists as people. The time to begin and whether college is needed follow in order. School counsellors handed it to cold war pupils eyeing science jobs.
43227-the-fundamentals-of-bacteriology:
Charles Bradfield Morrey, professor of bacteriology at Ohio State University, wrote The Fundamentals of Bacteriology for Lea and Febiger in 1921. This second edition, thoroughly revised, carries 171 engravings and six plates, with a portrait of Leeuwenhoek, who first saw bacteria, at the front. Morrey dedicates the book to his wife Grace, an American pianist, whose name the dedication carries for all readers.

Contents open with a historical introduction on spontaneous generation, putrefaction, and fermentation, then divide into form and structure, how bacteria live, and their study. Chapters treat cell walls, flagella, and spores, and the groupings of coccus, bacillus, and spirillum forms in their varied shapes. How bacteria live and grow covers growth conditions, food needs, and the making of acids, gases, enzymes, and toxins in turn. Disinfection and sterilisation take three chapters, down to the phenol coefficient.
43651-irish-witchcraft-and-demonology:
Irish Witchcraft and Demonology is a study of Irish witch trials and devil lore by Seymour, published at Dublin by Hodges, Figgis in 1913. The first chapter gives general remarks on witchcraft in Ireland. The author jokes that a famed chapter on snakes in Ireland held only the words that there are none, and asks whether witchcraft there is as thin a subject.

The chapters run by years. Dame Alice Kyteler, the sorceress of Kilkenny, fills the chapter for 1324. Surrounding cases cover Michael Scot, the enchanted Earl of Desmond, and sixteenth-century trials. Florence Newton, the witch of Youghal, follows for 1661, with the devil at Damerville after. Apparitions, charmed lives, and portents crowd the record.
43963-the-principles-of-stratigraphical-:
Marr, a fellow and lecturer at Cambridge, wrote a manual on the principles of stratigraphical geology. The book came out in 1898 in the Cambridge Natural Science Manuals. Marr wrote for students, and he left out much detail on single rock layers so the methods would stand clear.

Early chapters trace the growth of the science and the nature of layered rocks. Marr then sets out the law of superposition and the test of fossils held in the rocks. Later chapters treat the grouping of strata, maps and sections, and signs of the settings in which layers formed. The book then walks the column from the Precambrian and Cambrian up through the coal measures to the Pleistocene. Students got a compact guide to reading earth history from stacked stone.
44096-an-elementary-manual-of-new-zealan:
G V Hudson wrote An Elementary Manual of New Zealand Entomology, issued at London in eighteen ninety-two, with twenty-one coloured plates. Hudson gave the book to Lord Walsingham, a past head of the Entomological Society of London. The front plate shows a glow-worm in its stages.

Hudson aims to give the natural history of New Zealand's insects in plain words. He avoids needless hard terms for young collectors and general readers. Lists by Captain Broun and others, he notes, were too advanced for starters. Meyrick's works on moths and Enys's butterfly catalogue are named. Hudson hopes his book will fill the gap. He wants the study as loved in New Zealand as in Europe.
45229-mesopotamian-archaeology-an-introd:
Percy Handcock wrote this introduction to the archaeology of Babylonia and Assyria, published in London in 1912 with maps and many illustrations. Even the errata page is instructive, correcting dates of 2500 B C to 2400 B C at several points.

The contents move from land and people through a sketch of Babylonian and Assyrian history. Then come excavations, the decipherment of cuneiform, and chapters on architecture, sculpture, metallurgy, painting, and cylinder-seals. A final long chapter treats life, manners, customs, law, and religion, with a short bibliography and a king list. Students get the young science of Mesopotamian digging in one survey.
46609-the-book-lovers-anthology:
The Book-Lovers' Anthology, edited by Leonard, gathers prose and verse about books and reading. Henry Frowde published it for Oxford University Press in 1911. Its epigraph, taken from Montaigne in Florio's translation, admits the editor has only gathered a nosegay of strange flowers and supplied the thread to bind them.

The long list of acknowledgements shows the range of the picking. Leonard thanks publishers for Procter's piece called My Books, for Carlyle, for passages from Gissing's Private Papers of Henry Ryecroft, and for Stevenson's Picture Books in Winter. Whittier's poem The Library and pieces by Richard Jefferies also appear. The editor's stated ambition is modest: that book-lovers shall find the volume useful, and not without a charm of its own. He compares it to the patchwork the Hare brothers defended in a passage he quotes.
46643-pedagogical-anthropology:
Maria Montessori wrote Pedagogical Anthropology, shown here in English by Frederic Taber Cooper at New York in 1913 by Frederick A Stokes Company. One hundred and sixty three pictures and diagrams aid the text. Montessori had writ The Montessori Method. She gives the book to her mother and father on the forty fifth year of their union.

Contents treat modern trends in the study of man and their link to teaching. Old and new schools of that study are set out first. De Giovanni, Sergi, and Morselli and their schools get parts in turn. Method in the test sciences and the gathering of single facts hold the middle. The passage from analysis to synthesis and the limits of the field close the opening lectures. Child growth and measure in schools are the core theme.
46700-a-parody-anthology:
Carolyn Wells gathered A Parody Anthology, published by Charles Scribner's Sons of New York in 1919, from a 1904 copyright. She dedicated it to the wife of President Theodore Roosevelt. The volume belongs to her set of anthologies, of verse de société, whimsey, satire, and nonsense, each at a dollar and a half.

The note of thanks names the sources. Parodies from Bayard Taylor's Diversions of the Echo Club stand here by permission, with Sherman's Mary and Her Lamb from New Waggings of Old Tales. Owen Seaman contributes from In Cap and Bells and The Battle of the Bays. Ben King, James Whitcomb Riley, and Bunner are in the list, with Carman and Hovey's Staccato piece from Vagabondia. The Golfer's Rubaiyat turns Omar to the links. Readers get the art of the parody in its golden age, when every famous poem drew a witty twin.
47319-the-intrusions-of-peggy:
Anthony Hope, the author of The Prisoner of Zenda, wrote a light novel that Smith, Elder published in 1902. It opens on a changeful April morning. Trix Trevalla watches the river from her flat. For the first time in three years she has put off her widow's black, for a soft shade of blue.

Her maid is all in a flutter at the change. The widow recalls a childhood spent in a whirl of lodging houses. A baby brother died when she was six, too soft a child to live. The chapters ahead promise a dangerous game, a china vase, and a perjurer. A reconciliation closes the tale.
47528-a-satire-anthology:
Carolyn Wells gathered A Satire Anthology, published at New York in nineteen hundred and five. Wells thanked the many publishers who let her use their poems. A line from Lady Mary Wortley Montagu heads the book, praising satire as a keen, polished razor.

The set runs from Aristophanes and Horace to modern wits. Juvenal wishes for long life, and Ruteboeuf tells of an ass's legacy. Poems by Holmes, Lowell, Saxe, and Hay stand beside work by Crane, Gilman, and Burgess. Wells aimed for sharp verse that wounds with a touch barely felt. Old and new voices share the pages.
477-criminal-sociology:
Enrico Ferri, of the Italian school of criminology, argues that crime grows from social and physical causes as much as from individual choice. This preliminary text replaces a lost final version, and Ferri's argument still comes through clearly. Ferri, a student of Lombroso, pushed criminology toward social causes and reform.

Ferri weighs heredity, climate, poverty, and law, and he urges prevention and social reform over punishment alone. The book belongs beside Lombroso in the criminology series, and it shaped how later writers thought about crime. His school argued that punishment alone could not cure crime rooted in poverty and drink.
48059-a-vers-de-socie-te-anthology:
Carolyn Wells gathered A Vers de Societe Anthology, a book of light verse put out in New York in 1907. A line from Oliver Wendell Holmes heads the book. Holmes calls himself a florist in verse who must bring a bunch to each feast. Wells thanks a long list of firms for leave to use their poems.

The verse runs from Ben Jonson and a song by Shakespeare to verse of Wells own age. Songs from Twelfth Night and Much Ado sit near verse by Donne and Lodge. Later names include Longfellow, Whittier, Bret Harte, and Lewis Carroll. The poems are short, gay, and fit for a feast or a card. The set shows what light verse meant to hosts and guests of that time.
48225-collected-papers-on-analytical-psy:
C G Jung sets out his school of mind study in papers gathered for English readers in a Baillière second edition dated 1920. Constance E Long edited the authorised translation and wrote the preface to this reprint. Jung had held a post at the University of Zürich before his fame spread.

Long notes that the papers come from many sources and reach English readers here for the first time. Freud's works had crossed into English already, and Jung's Psychology of the Unconscious came out in America in 1916. Read with that book, these papers give a fair view of the Zürich school's ground, Long holds. Two new chapters, fourteen and fifteen, appear first in this edition with fresh thought from Jung.
4928-bulfinch-s-mythology:
Bulfinch's Mythology presents the classic retelling of ancient myth for readers who want the stories behind poetry and art. The religions of Greece and Rome are extinct as worship, the opening argues, but their gods survive in literature and taste, bound to the finest productions of ancient and modern imagination.

The volume gathers the Greek and Roman tales that poets, essayists, and orators constantly allude to, told in plain and entertaining prose. No author is named in the catalog record, though the collection is Bulfinch's standard work. Readers get a single handbook for the myths that underlie so much later writing.
50671-earth-features-and-their-meaning-a:
William Herbert Hobbs opens the study of rocks and landforms for students and general readers in a Macmillan text held under rights from 1912. Hobbs taught geology at the University of Michigan and had written on earthquakes and glaciers before. More than five hundred plates fill the book, starting with Mount Balfour and its glacier in the Selkirks.

Hobbs gives the book to the memory of George Huntington Williams on the dedication page. Chapter one treats how earth history is compiled, from its sources to the branches of geology as a science. Land features and what they mean form the core of the plan, Hobbs states at the start. A tabular recap closes the first chapter, which sets terms for all that follows.
51442-a-beginner-s-psychology:
Edward Bradford Titchener, a leading mind in the young science of psychology, wrote A Beginner's Psychology at New York in 1915. He gave the book to the memory of Thomas Henry Huxley. Its chapters open with what psychology is and does: common sense against science, the stuff the science treats, mind and body, and its ways of work. Then come sensation, simple image and feeling, attention, and perception.

Each part is split into short numbered sections, with questions and tasks at the end and lists of further reading. Titchener treats the senses of skin, taste, smell, ear, and eye in turn, then the marks and strength of sensation. The book was meant as a first door into the science for a new student, written by one of the men who had shaped how the subject was taught in America.
52414-the-christian-mythology:
Brigham Leatherbee wrote an attack on the Christian faith, sold at New York by the Truth Seeker Company. A motto at the head grants that knowledge is power. It adds that lack of knowledge is the mother of devotion. Thirteen chapters make up the book.

Heads name the virgin birth, pagan wonders, and false relics. Trial and death myths, twisted foretellings, and the rising from the dead follow. Wonders, the pardon bought by faith, and the three in one take their turns. Saints, good and evil spirits, feast days, and the supper close the list. Leatherbee opens by saying the faith of today stands far from what the first fathers taught.
53347-physiology:
M Foster writes an elementary text in Physiology, number six of the Science Primers edited by Professors Huxley, Roscoe and Balfour Stewart. D Appleton and Company published it at New York in 1877. A front plate explains the human skeleton in profile, labelling mandible, sternum, ribs, scapula, clavicle and the bones of arm and leg. Foster's preface calls the primer an introduction to Professor Huxley's Elementary Lessons.

He supposes the reader willing to handle a dead rabbit and a sheep's heart, holding observation as necessary to physiology as experiments are to chemistry. The senses are omitted so a few fundamental truths can be pressed with repetition.
54062-saunders-books-on-pathology-physio:
Saunders' Books on Pathology, Physiology, Histology, Embryology and Bacteriology is a publisher's catalogue from W B Saunders Company. The firm stood at 925 Walnut Street, Philadelphia, with a London house in Covent Garden. The catalogue was taken from the end of a 1908 textbook on diseases of women. A preface praises the house's judgment and modern business methods.

Listings start with the American Text-Book of Pathology, edited by Ludvig Hektoen and David Riesman. That book runs to 1245 pages with 443 pictures, 66 in colours, at $7.50 net in cloth. McConnell's Manual of Pathology follows, at 523 pages and $2.50 net. Praise from the Quarterly Medical Journal of Sheffield is quoted. The catalogue shows the range of a leading medical publisher.
54277-froebel-as-a-pioneer-in-modern-psy:
Froebel as a Pioneer in Modern Psychology, by Murray, was published at Baltimore by Warwick and York in 1914. Murray had written on infant schools and kindergartens before it. The book's claim is plain: Froebel's teaching rested on views of mind far more modern than most readers grant.

Chapter by chapter, Murray reads Froebel on the growth of mind, will, the first consciousness, and how feeling and sight of things unfold through action. Long chapters treat instinct, and play in its tie to work, and a further one sets out Froebel's play materials and their first purpose. Weak points are faced, and charges answered, in the closing chapters. Two appendices weigh the word activity and set Froebel's noted plays beside Groos's list. The study asks teachers to take Froebel as a thinker, not only a maker of gifts.
55974-anthropophagy:
Charles W Darling wrote Anthropophagy, a study of man-eating. T J Griffiths printed it at Utica in 1886. The book was printed in private, its page says. Darling served the Oneida Historical Society as secretary. Many state historical societies list him as member. The New England Historic Genealogical Society stands among them.

Wide reading on man's origins moved him to write, Darling says. Tales of man-eating crossed his pages again and again. The theme is unlovely and may repel some, he admits. He gathered the tales for his own amusement first. Teaching others came second in his aim. Faithfulness to the records is his sole merit claim. Classic myth opens the text proper after that. A gentleman antiquarian's grim hobby book shows how much strange lore a quiet library man could gather in 1886.
5614-chess-strategy:
Edward Lasker wrote Chess Strategy, translated by J. du Mont, in a second edition dated 1915, as a guide to playing chess well. The book contains 167 diagrams in ASCII line drawings, with a key explaining pieces and colors: rook, knight, bishop, queen, king, and pawn, with black pieces marked one way and white another. Rules and notation come first.

Later sections give hints for beginners, general principles of strategy, the opening, the endgame, and the middle game. Readers get a classic instruction book, clear and systematic, for players who want to think beyond single moves.
5694-the-harvard-classics-volume-38-scie:
Volume thirty-eight of the Harvard Classics gathers landmark papers on physiology, medicine, and the workings of the body. Its opening paper follows an early investigator of the heart. He turned to vivisection because books alone could not show when systole and diastole occur. He found the task arduous and full of difficulty. The volume's scope runs from Hippocrates, whose famous Oath is included, through later experimenters who tested ideas by direct observation.

Readers meet science in the act of learning: hypotheses are stated, animals are examined, and old authority is set against what the eye can see. The papers are demanding but rewarding, since each one shows a method as well as a result. For students of medicine and the history of science, this volume offers primary sources that still explain how modern physiology began to separate fact from received opinion.
57846-byways-in-british-archaeology:
Byways in British Archaeology gathers side path studies of old churches and customs, by Walter Johnson. Cambridge University Press published it in nineteen twelve, with many photographs. Johnson had written Folk Memory before turning to these church byways. Twelve chapters run from churches on pagan sites to a closing retrospect.

Two chapters show how churches rose where heathen worship stood before them. Two more treat the worldly uses of the church fabric through past ages. The facing of churches and of graves gets a chapter to each subject. Surviving burial customs and the lore of the four quarters follow in turn. The churchyard yew and the cult of the horse fill the later chapters. A final piece on the laboured ox closes the antiquary's tour.
57863-the-praise-of-shakespeare-an-engli:
The Praise of Shakespeare is an English anthology compiled by C E Hughes and published by Methuen of London in nineteen oh four. Sidney Lee, the great Shakespeare biographer, supplied the preface. The book collects what English writers have said in praise of Shakespeare across three hundred years.

Hughes arranges the tributes in periods, beginning with Francis Meres in fifteen ninety-six. The first period runs through Barnfield, Weever, Davies, and the First Folio voices of sixteen twenty-three. Ben Jonson, Hugh Holland, Heminge and Condell, Milton, Pepys, and Dryden all appear. Lee's notes on Shakespeare's reputation open the volume. Read in sequence, the extracts chart a reputation rising from fellow actor's playwright to national poet. Few anthologies show literary fame being built so plainly.
58109-history-of-biology:
Miall, once professor of biology at the University of Leeds, wrote History of Biology, published in London by Watts and Company in 1911. The book was issued for the Rationalist Press Association. Miall traces how the study of living things grew from ancient times to his own century.

The contents divide the story into periods. The first, from 1530 to 1660, covers the revival of botany and zoology and the rise of experimental physiology. Later periods treat the minute anatomists who worked with early microscopes, and the slow growth of system in naming plants and animals. A frontispiece shows Karl Ernst von Baer, a founder of embryology. Miall writes a short, clear survey for readers who want the main line of the science's past.
58924-the-crayfish-an-introduction-to-th:
Thomas Henry Huxley's monograph on the crayfish serves as an introduction to the study of zoology, taking one common animal as its whole subject. Huxley argues that a single creature, studied thoroughly, teaches the methods of the science. The crayfish is cheap, common, and complex enough to reward dissection. Its anatomy, life history, and kin are treated in order.

The book compares the crayfish with other crustaceans and with the lobster. Huxley's clear prose made it a student classic. It first appeared in a scientific series for general readers. Generations of biology students met zoology through this animal. The method, depth on one type, shaped laboratory teaching.
59074-australasian-fossils-a-students-ma:
Frederick Chapman wrote this guide to the old bones of the south lands for the use of the student. He was the man of old life at the National Museum in Melbourne. In past days he had done work in the part of the Royal College of Science in London that deals with rocks. The book is a hand book of the science of old life, made for the lands of Australasia.

A plate at the front shows a prize of the field: a stone lily of the old seas, near its true size. It lay in the mud stone of the Silurian age at Brunswick, in Victoria. The stone is kept at the museum in Melbourne.
59545-wrong-analogy:
Joseph Shallit wrote a tale of a new world gone sour called Wrong Analogy, first run in Worlds of If in August 1956. Ruth Flanders stands at a spaceport window with luggage piled round her, wild with joy at the fair land outside. Fields and orchards roll green and gold to a purple horizon, with pink and blue roofs among them.

Her husband Harvey fights his own joy down with care. Earth once had such places, in California and Florida, before the blight came. He begs her not to let hope run wild till they are sure all is well, for hope has been slapped down too often. The head note calls their guide a Pied Piper who changed his tune, and who must pay this time.
61386-post-biblical-hebrew-literature-an:
Halper, of Dropsie College, chose and turned into English a wide set of Hebrew works written after the Bible. The Jewish Publication Society of America issued the book at Philadelphia in 1921. Pieces range from the wisdom of Ben Sira to hymns, tales, and prayers.

Early pages hold sayings from the Mishnah and the Talmud, the death of Rabbi Akiba, and the death of Moses from the Midrash. Later come poets of Spain, among them Ibn Gabirol and Judah Halevi, with his Ode to Zion. Travel notes by Benjamin of Tudela and a tale of Moses as king of Cush show the breadth of the set.
61663-the-philosophy-of-biology:
The Philosophy of Biology is a thought tract by James Johnstone, a lore man of high mark. It came out at a great school press in nineteen fourteen. Its first part is named the world of thought. That parts sum tells that the live thing that knows is one that acts. Its sense of a world past it is not the mere fruit of the beats of that world on its sense tools.

It wakes full but to those beats that end in set acts of the flesh, that sum holds. That wake is its sight of the world it acts on. Its mind is a thick host of states, split past ease past the mind. That split lends size, span, and next place to the parts so split. Our sense of space is a gut sense and rests on our modes of flesh work, Johnstone holds.
62259-the-basis-of-social-relations-a-st:
Daniel G Brinton wrote The Basis of Social Relations, a study in ethnic psychology. Putnam’s Sons issued the book in New York in nineteen hundred two. It stands tenth in the Science Series of short learned books. Livingston Farrand of Columbia saw the dead author’s draft through print.

Brinton died in eighteen hundred ninety nine with the work near done. He had held the chair of American archaeology at Pennsylvania. His books on races, tongues, and old faiths won world wide fame. One rule guides all his work: the mind of man is one, he held. Farrand made small word fixes and slight shifts of parts here. Notes and sources stand just as the author left them, unrevised. How men group, rank, and hold to kin is the book’s great theme. Proof is drawn from tribes and nations round the whole earth.
62376-the-history-of-pedagogy:
History of Pedagogy, by Gabriel Compayre, traces teaching from the ancient world. Payne rendered the French work into English with notes and an index. Heath of Boston issued the translation in eighteen eighty nine. Compayre taught at the normal school of Fontenay aux Roses.

Chapters move from education in antiquity through Greece and Rome in turn. Early Christian and medieval schools form the next stage of the survey. Renaissance thought brings Erasmus, Rabelais, and Montaigne into the account here. Protestant work brings Luther and Comenius, then the Jesuit teaching orders. Readers get a full sweep of how schooling grew in the West.
62871-thoughts-on-a-pebble-or-a-first-le:
Thoughts on a Pebble, or A First Lesson in Geology is a short science book by Gideon Algernon Mantell, issued here in its eighth edition at London in 1849. Mantell, named on the frontispiece as a fellow of the Royal Society, wrote it as the author of The Wonders of Geology. He dedicated the little work to his son, Reginald Nebille Mantell.

The book takes a pebble picked up by a brook as its starting point. From that small stone it draws lessons about the whole earth. Mantell argues that no natural object is too small to teach great truths. Thirty-two pictures help make the geology plain for a young or new reader.
62923-the-rare-earths-their-occurrence-c:
S I Levy wrote The Rare Earths, their occurrence, chemistry, and technology, published at London in 1915 with illustrations. Levy was a late Hutchinson research student of St John's College, Cambridge. Part one treats the occurrence of the rare earths.

Chapters open with the nature of the minerals and how they occur. The silicates follow: cerite, gadolinite, allanite, and thortveitite among the yttrium and cerium metals, then thorite and zircon among thorium minerals. Titano-silicates and titanates come next, then the tantalo-columbates. Readers get an Edwardian chemist's field guide to the strangest corner of the periodic table, written when the rare earths were still being prised apart one salt at a time.
63089-the-body-at-work-a-treatise-on-the:
Alex Hill, once master of Downing College, Cambridge, wrote The Body at Work, a treatise on the principles of physiology printed in London in 1908. Forty-six illustrations go with the text. Photographs of cells from the cortex of the brain, much enlarged, form the frontispiece. Opening chapters treat first principles, the basis of life, and the unit of structure.

The fluids of the body and the inner secretions follow, then digestion at length. Breathing and the casting out of waste come next, then the circulation of the blood. Muscle and the nervous system fill the long middle of the book. Smell and taste, vision, hearing, the feelings of the skin, and voice and speech close the survey of the working body.
63311-methods-aims-in-archaeology:
Methods and Aims in Archaeology is a field manual by W M Flinders Petrie. Macmillan published it in London and New York in 1904. Petrie wrote from two decades of digging in Egypt. He dedicates the book to the friends who joined his work between 1884 and 1903. The names include H Carter, B P Grenfell, and J E Quibell.

The chapters follow a dig from start to finish. Petrie sets out the character an excavator needs. He teaches discrimination between temples, towns, and cemeteries. Labourers, overseers, day pay, and piecework get a practical chapter. Field recording, planning, and plotting follow. Copying, photographing, and preservation each have their own methods. A final run of chapters covers packing and transport. Sixty-six illustrations show the work, from a chain of boys clearing the Osireion at Abydos onward.
65151-how-old-is-it-the-story-of-dating-:
How Old Is It is a short guide to the dating of old things by James Schoenwetter. The book is the second in a set of small works from a state museum. Its field has a long name for the science of time marks in the earth. Few hands in the world hold skill in all the ways of that trade.

Two kinds of clocks rule the field in the first talk of the book. One ticks at a set rate and gives a true count of years past. The next ticks now and then and gives just a place in a chain. Dig men pick the clock that fits the tale they need to tell. Tree rings and ash beds earn their parts in the plain guide.
65566-porgy:
Porgy is the novel by Du Bose Heyward, published by the George Doran Company in New York in 1925 and dedicated to Dorothy Heyward. Theodore Nadejen supplied the decorations. A verse prelude names the cast: Porgy, Maria, and Bess, Robbins, and Peter, and Crown. Life, it says, was a three-stringed harp brought from the woods to town.

The novel opens by placing Porgy in a golden age of an ancient, beautiful city that time forgot. Charleston is meant. In those days beggary was a profession with a tradition, and a plea brought a coin rather than a file of papers. Porgy the crippled beggar stands at the center of the tenement world the book makes famous. Heyward's novel later carried its story to the stage and the opera house, but the book itself remains the source.
65807-the-new-poetry-an-anthology:
Harriet Monroe and Alice Corbin Henderson, the editors of Poetry magazine, gathered an anthology of the new poetry. It was first published in 1917 and reissued at New York in 1920 with a revised bibliography. An editor's note on typography disclaims any rigid system: each poet's own lineation and indention stand, sonnets indented or not as their authors prefer.

The contents open with Conrad Aiken's music heard and dancing Adairs, pass through Zoë Akins and Richard Aldington's images, and reach Rupert Brooke's sonnets of nineteen-fourteen. Imagists, free-versifiers, and rhymesters share the pages without apology for their spelling of gray or grey. The little-magazine movement, bound between boards, is the volume.
66033-direct-conversion-of-energy:
Direct Conversion of Energy is a booklet by William R Corliss, issued by the United States Atomic Energy Commission. It belongs to a series called Understanding the Atom. A foreword signed by the commission's information director opens it. Nuclear energy plays a vital role in the life of every American today, that note says. Citizens must understand it to discharge their duties thoughtfully, it argues.

Contents treat direct against dynamic conversion first, then the laws governing conversion. Thermoelectricity and thermionic conversion follow. Magnetohydrodynamic conversion takes a chapter of its own. Chemical batteries and the fuel cell, a continuously fueled battery, come next. Solar cells, nuclear batteries, and advanced concepts close the list.
66246-our-atomic-world-the-story-of-atom:
Craven wrote Our Atomic World, the story of atomic energy, for the United States Atomic Energy Commission in its Understanding the Atom series. A foreword says nuclear energy plays a vital part in the life of every man, woman, and child in the United States today. Citizens need a sound grasp of this force, the foreword holds, to do their duties well and reap its many gains. The cover shows a time-exposed model of a uranium-235 atom.

Contents run from the Greeks, who were curious about matter, to the proof of the atomic theory and the finding of the nucleus by Rutherford. Protons, isotopes, and particles with no electric charge follow. Fission is explained and the fission bomb told of, then the need for nuclear energy in the years ahead. Fusion, the uses of isotopes, the Commission itself, and a move toward an international atom close the book.
67172-a-guide-to-mythology:
Helen Clarke wrote this guide to mythology for young readers, published by Doubleday, Page in a 1918 Garden City edition of a 1908 book. Her aim, she says, is solid knowledge based on the most recent work of scholars, taught through stories that will lay a firm foundation for comparative mythology later. She thanks many publishers and authors for leave to retell their tales, from Leland's Algolquin legends and Bryant's Odyssey to Grey's Polynesian myths.

Her debts to scholars run from Max Müller and Frazer's Golden Bough to Fiske, Lang, and Hartland. The frontispiece shows Automedon with the horses of Achilles, from a painting by Regnault. Clarke had already written Ancient Myth in Modern Poets and books on the country of Longfellow and Hawthorne. She dedicates the guide to her little friend Katharine Corfield Newbold.
69053-the-conservation-of-energy:
Balfour Stewart wrote The Conservation of Energy, a plain guide to a great law. The book stands seventh in the International Scientific Series. D Appleton and Company issued the set in New York. Stewart taught natural philosophy at Owens College in Manchester.

One law rules the whole tale: force is never lost, it holds. Heat, light, work, and life draw on one shared world store. Spend it here and it shows there, in a new dress each time. An added part treats the law in flesh and mind at the end. Tyndall on water and Bagehot on politics stand near in the set. Spencer, Bain, and Cooke share the same plain, cheap shelf line. Each book cost a dollar and a half in cloth in those years. Clear short books for lay readers were the set’s whole aim.
69557-a-definition-of-social-work-a-thes:
A Definition of Social Work, a thesis in sociology by Alice Cheyney, was presented in 1923. She offered it to the graduate school of the University of Pennsylvania for her doctorate. Why this definition is attempted opens the contents at page five. The charitable element in social work follows as chapter two of the thesis.

The scientific element in social work forms the third chapter of her argument. Testimony of the national conference of social work fills chapter four of the work. Testimony of the training schools for professional workers comes next in the contents. The answer to its critics closes the main text before an appendix and bibliography. What social worker has not been asked to define social work, she opens by asking.
70275-mrs-gurney-s-apology:
William Brotherhead printed this odd pamphlet at Philadelphia in 1860. Its title is Mrs Gurney's Apology, and its stated aim is to back the friendship of a Mrs whose name is left blank. The publisher's own preface washes his hands of the whole affair.

He calls the piece a strange writing and a great outrage on public feeling. He denies any backing for the writer's views and laments the scandal. The row touched the Society of Friends and great houses in England and America, he says. The Gurney name, he notes, stands for good works on both sides of the sea. Readers get a rare window on a Victorian scandal in print.
70448-tokology:
Tokology is a health book for each woman by Alice Stockham, a cure trained hand. Its next name calls it just that, a book for every woman in full. A Fenno house of New York brought out this changed print of the work. First right claims run back to eighteen eighty three in its leaves. She gives the book to her girl child and to all women who heed it.

Pain free birth heads part one with word from roam folk and cure men. Womb growth, seed law, and babe blood flow fill part two in rank. Signs of the state, quick stir, and heart beat fill part three. Ills of the state, sick gut, and bad food fill part four scheme. True food and right life are its cure for the woes of her sex.
70963-heortology:
A history of the Christian festivals by K A Heinrich Kellner. Kegan Paul published the English translation at London in 1908. Kellner taught Catholic theology at the University of Bonn. A priest of the Westminster diocese translated the second German edition. Church censors approved both editions, and their stamps appear in front. The title's Greek root means the study of feasts.

Kellner's preface states the need for the book. Older liturgy works treated festivals inside larger wholes. Recent articles lit single points but left others dark. New documents had lately reshaped the field. The Peregrinatio Silviae and old lectionaries supplied fresh evidence. Kellner gathers the solid results for students and younger clergy. Christmas, Easter, and the saints' days all gain a documented history.
71116-practical-pathology:
Practical Pathology: A Manual of Autopsy and Laboratory Technique for Students and Physicians, by Aldred Scott Warthin, professor of pathology at the University of Michigan. George Wahr issued the manual at Ann Arbor in 1911. The second edition was rewritten and enlarged to 310 pages with 55 figures, under the motto Mortui vivos docent, the dead teach the living.

Warthin's preface says the first edition sold out despite its typographic errors. His autopsy method is a composite of the Rokitansky, Virchow, Chiari, and Nauwerck methods, chosen for speed and ease of performance. Part two sets out the bench steps for close work with the microscope.
71233-anthropology:
Anthropology, an introduction to the study of man and civilization, is a work by Edward Tylor, printed at London in 1881 with pictures. Tylor's preface takes up a doubt at once: in an age of multiplied studies, is it fair to lay a new science on the pressed student? His answer is that anthropology lightens the load rather than adding to it.

He likens the science to the carrying frame that mountain bearers shoulder beside their burdens, since it holds the load together and balances it. By tracing how each art arose from the simple wants of early man, the learner grasps it from the beginning instead of the middle. Gesture and cries lead on to speech, and grammar loses its air of arbitrary rules.
71234-some-possible-bearings-of-genetics:
Thomas Hunt Morgan, professor of experimental zoology at Columbia University, gave the Middleton Goldsmith Lecture before the New York Pathological Society on February 3, 1922. It was printed at Lancaster the same year. His theme is what the young science of genetics may bear upon the study of disease.

Morgan begins by answering a sneer: that genetics deals mostly with albinos, dwarfs, freaks, and the like, and so cannot be of the first importance. Such material, he replies, is pathological in a broad sense already. The geneticist, he notes, cares less for a character's nature than for its mode of inheritance, and knows each defect has a normal partner in the germ-plasm.
71245-the-new-buggy:
New Buggy, by Aunt Hattie, is a boys tale in the Happy Home Stories. Madeline Leslie wrote under that pen name for young readers at home. Young of Boston issued the volume, entered in eighteen seventy one. The set for boys also holds Diligent Dick and Lazy Robert.

Chapters open with truant boys and what happened next on their path. Daniel and his father, a troubled conscience, and another lie follow. A distracted mother, a senseless boy, and forgiveness build the moral arc. The doctor bill and Jimmy plan close the short tale out. A Paul text on kindness and forgiveness fronts the book as motto.
71454-guide-to-the-study-of-animal-ecolo:
Guide to the Study of Animal Ecology is a textbook by Charles Adams, of the department of zoology at the University of Illinois. Macmillan published it in New York in 1913. Ecology was then a young science, and Adams wrote to give its students a method. A photograph of an oyster bank in South Carolina, a true animal community, faces the title page.

The early chapters set out the aim and point of view of the science and the value of ecological surveys. Field study follows, then the collection, preservation, and naming of specimens.
