The oyster bank serves as the model case: many kinds of animals living together between the tides, each shaped by the place and by the others. Adams argues that animals must be studied where they live, as members of communities, not as pinned specimens alone.
71827-anthropology:
Kroeber wrote a textbook of anthropology printed at New York in 1923. Chapter one sets the scope and character of the science: anthropology, biology, and history, its organic and social parts, and its physical and cultural sides. The age of the science and the fanciful side of evolution talk are weighed. Chapter two turns to fossil man.

The missing link, the family tree of the primates, glacial time, and the place of man's origin come first. Pithecanthropus, Heidelberg man, the Piltdown form, Neandertal man, Rhodesian man, and the Cro Magnon race follow in order. Chapter three sorts living races and the traits on which sorting rests. Students get the whole young science in one ordered book, from bones to languages and customs.
71984-an-introductory-lecture-on-arch-ol:
Churchill Babington delivered An Introductory Lecture on Archæology before the University of Cambridge, printed at the University Press in eighteen sixty five. Babington was Disney Professor of Archæology and senior fellow of St John College. The lecture was divided in the delivery into two parts. Illustrative specimens were exhibited after each portion, the preface says. Book lists for particular branches close the work.

The Rev T G Bonney and the Rev W G Searle helped draw up certain of the lists, Babington thanks them. For ancient art and archæology K O Müller Manual will in general sufficiently indicate the bibliography, he says. Only in a few departments, in numismatics more especially, was it deemed necessary to add anything, he notes. Students get a Victorian professor map of the young science of archaeology, from coins to ancient art.
72158-history-of-anthropology:
History of Anthropology, by Alfred Haddon with Hingston Quiggin, surveys the field. Watts and Company issued it at London from Johnson Court, Fleet Street. A portrait of Tylor fronts the book as its founding figure plate. Contents split the field into physical study and wider human science in turn.

Early chapters trace pioneers from Hippocrates and Aristotle to Blumenbach and Linnæus. Skull study, the cephalic index, and body measures get a full chapter. Debates on the origin of man run from Monboddo to Darwin Origin of Species. Fossil finds at Neanderthal and Spy unfold the antiquity of man next. Comparative psychology, eugenics, and race classification follow in the scheme.
73338-beginners-zoology:
Walter Coleman's Beginners' Zoology was authorized by the Minister of Education for Ontario and published by the Macmillan Company of Canada in Toronto in nineteen twenty-one. Its first chapter lays down the principles of biology. Biology, from Greek words for life and discourse, is the science of life, and zoology is its animal branch. Living things differ from the lifeless by their functions: feeding, growth, development, and multiplication.

Fourteen chapters climb the animal ladder in teaching order. Protozoans, sponges, polyps, echinoderms, and worms lead to crustaceans and a long insect section. Molluscs, fishes, frogs and their kin, reptiles, birds, and mammals finish the course. Organs, the book explains, are parts with set work to do, and both plants and animals count as organized beings for that reason.
73420-research-methods-in-ecology:
Frederic Edward Clements wrote Research Methods in Ecology. The University Publishing Company issued it at Lincoln, Nebraska in 1905. Clements taught plant physiology at that university. Irving S Cutter shares the copyright with him. Chapter One lays the base of the field. The scope of ecology leads its heads.

Ecology and physiology stand side by side early on. Plant grouping and plant succession get early heads. The habitat fills Chapter Two in full. Its factors are named, classed, and weighed. Clements presses the lack of trained men in the field. Plain survey work still rules, he notes. Field men, foresters, and soil men all touch the field, he says. A founding manual, the book gave plant ecology a strict method while the science was still young.
73427-elements-of-agricultural-chemistry:
Johnston gave these lectures on agricultural chemistry and geology, reader in chemistry and mineralogy at the University of Durham. Suggestions for experiments in practical agriculture are added to the lectures. The publisher's notice says the course would run to four parts in two volumes, the first part now ready.

Part one treats the organic parts of plants. Its lectures name the simple stuffs plants live on, the compounds that feed their growth, and where plants get their food. They trace how food enters a plant's circulation and what it becomes inside. Part two turns to the mineral parts of plants, then to soils: their origin, kinds, and makeup, and how geology bears on farming and soil improvement.
74049-anthropology:
Anthropology is a lecture by Franz Boas, professor at Columbia University. He gave it on December 18, 1907, in a series on science, philosophy, and art. Columbia University Press issued it in print in 1908. Boas opens by admitting his task is beset with difficulties. His field studies man from the biological, geographical, and psychological points of view. Those lines of research can look split and without unity.

Boas explains the aims that bind them into one science. The field does not study man as a lone individual. It studies how traits differ between groups of men. Climate, place, and past history shape those groups. The lecture asks what causes brought about the observed differences. It also traces the sequence of events behind the many forms of human life. In short, the lecture is a map of a young science.
74485-a-handy-dictionary-of-mythology:
Whittaker's handy dictionary of mythology offers everyday readers concise accounts of the gods and goddesses of the ancients. It belongs to the Familiar Quotations series, priced at one shilling in cloth or one and sixpence half-bound.

The preface argues that these deities meet us at every turn in museums and galleries, and live in the allusions of poets, painters, and comic papers. A Punch cartoon of the Judgment of Paris, with living lords cast as Juno, Minerva, and Venus, shows why a quick reference helps. The author also wrote handy books of synonyms, proverbs, and daily blunders. Clark of Edinburgh printed the little volume.
74532-outlines-of-mineralogy:
Outlines of Mineralogy is a system by Torbern Bergman of Upsala, in an English translation of 1783. Withering, a physician of Edinburgh medical society, translated the work for this edition. It was printed at Birmingham by Piercy and Jones for Cadell in London and Balfour and Elliott in Edinburgh. A motto from Ovid on digging into the bowels of the earth heads the title.

The translator preface says the pleasure and instruction he received from this excellent little work inspired his wish. He wished to make it more generally known to others by his translation of its pages. It never can be exploded, he adds in praise of Bergman method of the work. Bergman chemistry of minerals was a foundation of the science, and Withering, himself a mineralogist and the introducer of digitalis, was its fit English voice.
74804-text-book-of-forensic-medicine-and:
Buchanan, professor of forensic medicine at the University of Liverpool, issued the eighth edition of his text-book in 1915, revised and enlarged. The first part covers legal medicine for doctors who may face a courtroom, from court procedure and medical evidence to sudden death and post-mortem work. Later chapters treat wounds, blood stains, drowning, and the signs of death.

The second part turns to poisons and how they act on the body. Buchanan explains how poisoning is proved, how a case should be treated, and how tests are made for the poison itself. Fingerprint figures and plates of bone growth show the close detail expected of a working reference for doctors and lawyers.
74836-mexican-arch-ology:
Mexican Archaeology, by Thomas Joyce, is an introduction to the archaeology of the Mexican and Mayan civilizations of pre Spanish America. It was published in New York and London in 1914, with many illustrations and a map. Joyce had also written a South American archaeology volume.

Contents march in parallel halves. For Mexico: tribal history, the gods, the calendar and calendrical feasts. Then writing, priesthood, medicine, and burial. The social system, war, trade, and justice follow. Crafts, dress, daily life, architectural remains, and pottery close the Mexican half. The Maya half repeats the plan: history, religion and myth, the calendar, burial and society, dress and crafts, and architecture. Appendices give the names of the days and months in both calendars. A front picture shows a mosaic skull held by the British Museum. Readers get the standard English handbook of its day.
75183-the-eatonville-anthology:
Zora Neale Hurston wrote The Eatonville Anthology, printed in The Messenger across September, October, and November 1926. Short sketches paint life in Eatonville, a Black town in Florida. Hurston renders the talk of its people in dialect.

First comes the pleading woman, Mrs Tony Roberts, who begs meat and greens door to door though her larder is full. Tony, her husband, is the best provider on the store's list, yet she sings that he does not feed her. A second sketch, Turpentine Love, tells how a spill of turpentine cured a wife's fits. Each piece is brief, fond, and comic.
75254-physico-theology:
Physico-Theology is a set of sermons by Derham on God in nature. Derham was canon of Windsor and rector of Upminster in Essex. He was a fellow of the Royal Society as well. The sermons were preached at Saint Mary le Bow in London. They formed the Boyle lectures in the years 1711 and 1712.

Their full title promises a proof of the being and attributes of God. That proof rests on his works of creation in the world. Large notes and many curious observations swell the printed sermons here. Earthquakes, fossils, animals, and the heavens give Derham his texts in turn. Natural theology argued design from nature long before Darwin's day came.
76851-first-course-in-biology:
First Course in Biology is a school textbook issued by the Macmillan Company for young students of life science. Part one, on plant biology, is the work of Bailey, a famed name in plant study. Part two treats animal biology, and part three the human body. A front picture shows a Kentish plover with eggs and young.

That picture is used to teach protective resemblance in nature. The bird and its eggs blend with the ground in the museum case shown. A first course must start with such clear sights, the book holds. Plants come first, then animals, then man, in the old order of the science. Classes across America learned their biology from books of this build. Text, pictures, and questions led the pupil step by step.
77045-agricultural-zoology:
Ritzema Bos, a lecturer at the Royal Agricultural College at Wageningen in Holland, wrote a survey of animals for farm students. Ainsworth Davis translated it, and Eleanor Ormerod wrote the introduction. The London edition of 1894 holds one hundred forty nine illustrations. Bos meant it as a condensed review of the whole animal kingdom for agricultural colleges.

Animals harmful or helpful to agriculture get the fullest treatment. Farm stock is left out, since stock breeding lecturers cover it elsewhere. Bos hopes the practical farmer can also use the book in private. German roots show in its full handbook on pests and helpers for field, herd, forest, and garden. Measures to destroy pests and protect crops close each account.
78985-an-introduction-to-philology:
An Introduction to Philology, subtitled The Science of Language, is a popular primer by Clement Wood. It appeared as Little Blue Book Number 708, from the Haldeman-Julius Company of Girard, Kansas, in 1924. The Little Blue Books sold short, cheap classics and handbooks by mail.

Wood begins by asking what philology is: the study of human speech, the science of language. Four chapters follow. The first traces the sources of our words, from the Teutonic and French elements to the classical ones. The second treats the formation of words, with folk etymology and word creation. The third follows the behaviour of words: the words for colours, euphemism and exaggeration, and how meanings widen, narrow, sink or rise. The last chapter, the romance of words, takes up place names, personal names, and the American language itself.
79014-gestalt-psychology:
Wolfgang Kohler wrote a book on Gestalt psychology, printed at New York in 1929. It went through four printings in its first year. The book is given to Max Wertheimer. I offer this book to the patient reader, feeling more than ever how much I have been inferior to my task, Kohler begins. Nothing is easier than to criticize it.

Gestalt psychology, the subject I have tried to present, resembles in 1928 a promising start more than a complete achievement, he owns. To present it well in a foreign language was beyond his power, he adds. Only simple and almost crude concepts of the school would yield to his efforts in English. Behaviorism and introspection are weighed beside the new German school. The whole is more than the sum of its parts, argued here for English readers.
9380-a-nonsense-anthology:
Carolyn Wells collected this nonsense anthology in 1910, dedicated to Gelett Burgess, a nonsense lover. Its motto, from William Rolfe, holds that he who cannot play the fool at times lacks sense. The crown jewel is Lewis Carroll's Jabberwocky, with slithy toves, mome raths, and the frumious Bandersnatch, slain by a vorpal blade.

Anonymous verse joins the famous pieces, all in praise of gleeful absurdity. Wells arranged the book as a feast, not a lesson. It remains a delightful shelf of nonsense, for children and for grown-ups who still enjoy a good burble.
a-nonsense-anthology: Carolyn Wells gathers comic verse in this anthology, opening with Jabberwocky and its slithy toves, mome raths, and frumious Bandersnatch. Dedicated to Gelett Burgess, a fellow lover of nonsense, the collection treats playful foolishness as a sign of sense rather than its absence. It quotes William Rolfe's remark that a man who never plays the fool lacks sense, and its pleasures are verbal: invented words, absurd images, and rhymes that refuse to behave.
aids-to-forensic-medicine-and-toxicology: William George Aitchison Robertson sets out a compact aid to forensic medicine and toxicology for medical students facing the triple board examinations. The book covers wounds, poisons, and the signs by which a doctor judges cause of death, with the examiner's needs kept in view throughout. In its ninth edition, it served as a clear, exam-ready summary of a field where medicine meets the law.
american-addresses-with-a-lecture-on-the: Thomas Henry Huxley delivers American addresses with a lecture on the study of biology, opening with three hypotheses about the history of nature. He then sets out the neutral and favourable evidence for evolution, closing with demonstrative evidence for the theory. The lectures show Huxley at his clearest, defending Darwin before American audiences in plain, forceful prose.
anthropology: Robert Ranulph Marett writes Anthropology in the Home University Library of Modern Knowledge, under editors including Herbert Fisher and Gilbert Murray. The little book surveys human origins, customs, and beliefs for general readers. Marett's clear summary introduced a new science to a wide public in compact form. Its short span makes a fine first step.
apology:
Plato gives Socrates' defense speech at his trial in Athens, translated by Benjamin Jowett, with an introduction weighing how close the speech stands to what Socrates really said. Socrates stands accused of corrupting the young and denying the gods. He answers by cross-examining his accuser and telling the story of his life.

He explains the oracle that called him wisest, his testing of politicians, poets, and craftsmen, and the divine sign that guides him. Offered chances to beg, flee, or fall silent, he refuses each one. The speech closes with his calm talk of death as either sleep or a passage to better company. It remains a founding text of philosophy.
b09-melanchthon-apology:
The Apology of the Augsburg Confession is Philipp Melanchthon's defense of his confession, written in 1531. Catholic scholars at Augsburg had drawn up a refutation of the Lutheran articles. Melanchthon answered it point by point, at greater length and with sharper argument than the confession itself.

The Apology presses hardest on how a sinner stands right before God, by faith in Christ alone. It ranges across repentance, good works, the mass, and the saints. Lutherans count it among their core confessional books. The translation here is by F Bente and W H T Dau. Few works show Melanchthon's learning and care for clear teaching so fully.
biology:
Edmund Beecher Wilson delivered this lecture at Columbia University in November 1907, in the series on science, philosophy, and art, and the Columbia University Press printed it in 1908. Wilson, professor of zoology and America's leading cell biologist, begins with a caution: no single science may properly claim the name biology exclusively. The word is a generic term for the sciences of the living world, not one discipline's property.

His theme is explanation's limit. Some phenomena of life, able naturalists had lately argued, cannot by their nature receive a rational account along physico-chemical or mechanistic lines. In face of such a case the mechanist must confess himself brought to a standstill, Wilson admits — and then argues for patience rather than vitalism. The lecture maps the mechanism-versus-vitalism debate at the moment genetics was about to settle parts of it.
brief-reflections-relative-to-the-emigra:
Fanny Burney published Brief Reflections relative to the Emigrant French Clergy in London in 1793, signing herself the author of Evelina and Cecilia. Burney gives the tract's profits wholly to relief of the French clergy driven out by revolution. Her plea is aimed at the ladies of Great Britain.

Six thousand clergy shelter in England, Burney states, against far larger hosts abroad. Age unhonoured and disease unattended fill her charge against delay. She asks for deeds, not tears, and prints plans for relief at the back. An apology first clears her right, as a woman, to speak on a public sorrow. The tract shows a famed novelist turning her pen to charity in a refugee crisis, with plain counts of the need.
britannica-1911-adonis-mythology:
Adonis, in Greek and Roman myth, was a youth of striking beauty loved by Aphrodite. One account makes him the son of a Syrian king by his own daughter. That daughter, Smyrna, had been driven by the goddess to an unnatural love. When the king learned the truth he would have slain her at once. The gods in pity changed her into a tree of her name.

After ten months the tree burst open and Adonis came forth from it. Aphrodite, charmed by his beauty, hid the baby in a box for safety. She gave him to Persephone to keep, who then refused to return him. Zeus settled the dispute by a ruling on the year. Adonis would spend a third with each goddess, and a third as his own. He was later killed by a boar sent by Artemis.
britannica-1911-algae-ecology:
Ecology, a section of the Algae article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, asks how algal form matches conditions of life. Among land plants, similar environments call out similar adaptations in widely separated families, as desert spurges come to resemble cacti. The section tests whether the same holds in the water. Strikingly similar forms do appear in distant algal groups, and paired examples are listed.

Blue-green Gloeocapsa mirrors green Gloeocystis, red Batrachospermum mirrors green Draparnaldia, and the green sea lettuce Ulva mirrors red Porphyra. Yet similar forms also seem to grow apart under like conditions, so the section warns that trustworthy general rules are hard to reach. Water's chemistry, fresh, brackish, or salt, its movement, and the light reaching each depth all count as conditions. The laws governing which algae gather together under one environment, the entry admits, are as yet little understood.
britannica-1911-analogy:
Analogy, from a Greek word for proportion, is a term with several distinct uses. The entry works through them in order. In general, it means resemblance that falls short of complete similarity or identity. A word like loud can pass from sounds to garments. All metaphor counts as a kind of analogy. Euclid used the term for proportionate equality. In mathematics it now survives mainly in the phrase Napier's Analogies.

Grammar uses analogy for similarity in a language's patterns of derivation and spelling. In logic, it names inference from known resemblances to unobserved cases. Aristotle treated such reasoning under the heading of example. The entry sets out Kant's and Hamilton's attempts to separate analogy from induction. Mill rejects that sharp separation as artificial. Kant's Analogies of Experience close the survey. They cover substantiality, causality, and reciprocity, the give-and-take between things.
britannica-1911-antenor-mythology:
Antenor is a myth article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about one of the wisest elders of Troy in Greek legend. He advised his fellow townsmen to send Helen back to her husband. He showed himself not unfriendly to the Greeks and a friend of peace. Homer names him among the elders on the wall of Troy.

Later story took a darker turn. In the accounts of Dares and Dictys, Antenor was said to have opened the gates of Troy to the enemy by treachery. In return, at the sack of the city, the victors spared his house. A panther's skin at the door marked it out. After the fall, the tales split. In one he rebuilt a city on the site of Troy, in another he settled at Cyrene, and in a third he founded Patavium.
britannica-1911-anthology:
An anthology, in its root sense, is a garland or gathering of flowers. The word is used in a figure for any choice set of fine pieces of writing. It points most of all to the Greek Anthology, a great body of short poems. That body holds about four thousand five hundred pieces in all. More than three hundred writers are named among its makers.

Greek poets wrote short verse for set occasions from an early age. Such verse marked famed persons or events, on tombs and on gifts to the gods. Those pieces were called epigrams, meaning inscriptions cut in stone. An inscription had to be brief by its nature. That need, with Greek taste, set the marks of the style. Brevity, weight of sense, pure wording, and one clear thought were all required.
britannica-1911-anthropology:
Anthropology is defined in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica from two Greek words for man and for study. In its strict sense it is the study of man as a unit in the world of beasts. That sets it apart from the study of man as a stock unit. It sets it apart as well from the study of how stocks are spread on the earth.

In its wide sense the word names the whole life tale of man. In that sense both kin fields form part of it, as parts form a whole. More fields still stand in its train. The study of the frame of the body is one. The study of the mind at work is a second. The study of tongues is named in the same train. The entry draws a map of a wide field and its parts.
britannica-1911-apology:
Apology, from a Greek word for a defence, means in its common sense a show of regret. It owns that a thing was said or done in the wrong. It can also be a pulling back of a charge that is false. In a suit for libel, the fact that a full and prompt apology was made counts to cut the damages. The apology should have the same reach as the charge that it seeks to mend.

If the charge was made in public, the right form is a note in a newspaper. If it was heard by a few, a letter that can be read to those who heard it may do. The Libel Act of 1843 set a rule for libel in a newspaper. A man may plead that the words went in with no true ill will and no gross lack of care.
britannica-1911-bacteriology:
Bacteriology is the science of bacteria, the minute organisms also loosely called microbes or micro-organisms. The entry, a very long one, splits in two: a first part on the general study of bacteria, and a second on their medical side. Botanists' preferred name for the organisms themselves, it notes, is schizomycetes, Nägeli's term of 1857.

Bacteria are described as tiny plant-like cells without chlorophyll, the green matter of plants, multiplying by splitting in two, in shapes round, oblong, rod-like, or in threads. Fifty years earlier they were mere microscope curiosities, confused with other small life, their life history unknown. By the entry's day hundreds of forms were described, whole laboratories and libraries served the subject, and its branches in medicine, farming, and sewage work had grown into studies of their own.
britannica-1911-bed-geology:
Bed, in the study of rocks, is a term explained in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It names kinds of rock most often found laid out in clear layers. Those layers are the beds of rock, also called strata by geologists. In the normal case the bedding of rocks lies flat or near flat across the ground.

When the top and base of a bed run parallel, the bedding is called regular. If a bed is thickest at one point and thins away in all ways, it is lenticular. Beds may run fifty feet thick or more at the grand end. At the fine end they thin to sheets like paper, as in paper shales. Such thin beds are often called layers or laminae by workers. Mid kinds go by names like flags and flagstones. Fine grained rocks bed more thinly and evenly than coarse sandstones and grits.
britannica-1911-biology:
Biology is the science of living matter, from the Greek bios, life. The 1911 Britannica article opens by setting its borders with care. Psychology and sociology touch it closely, yet custom groups them apart. No natural boundary truly splits them from biology, the article argues. Social life in animals, at times shadowing human policy, falls squarely to the biologist. The sharp line runs between living and not-living matter instead.

Living matter is marked off by a list of special properties. Its chemistry, growth, and response set it apart from all other things. No link between the living and the not-living is known at present, the article states. The long piece then maps the science's branches and sister articles. Cytology covers cells, embryology covers development, and heredity and reproduction cover parent and offspring. Huxley and Mitchell share the byline at the close.
britannica-1911-clergy:
Clergy is a collective term signifying in English strictly the body of clerks, that is, men in holy orders, from forms traced through French to Low Latin. Older Middle English senses of clerkship and learning have long fallen obsolete, the entry notes. Modern use widens the word beyond technical clerks to embrace all varieties of ordained Christian ministers. Yet clergyman in the United Kingdom still marks clergy of the Established Church against the word minister.

As applied to the Roman Catholic Church the word embraces the whole hierarchy, whether in holy orders or merely in minor orders. Loose use for members of regular orders is improper, since monks and friars as such have never been clerici. Against the clergy stands the laity, from a Greek word for people, the great body of the faithful. That flock and shepherd relation frames the distinctions the entry then pursues at length.
britannica-1911-daphne-mythology:
Daphne, whose name is the Greek word for a laurel tree, was in Greek myth the daughter of the Arcadian river-god Ladon, or of the Thessalian Peneus, or of the Laconian Amyclas. Apollo loved her, and as he pursued her she was changed by her mother Gaea into a laurel tree, which stayed sacred to the god. Ovid tells the tale in the Metamorphoses.

The Peloponnesian legends give Daphne another suitor, Leucippus, son of Oenomaus of Pisa. He dressed as a girl and joined her companions to stay near her. While they bathed, his sex was found out, and the nymphs killed him. The entry cites Pausanias and Parthenius for that darker version of the story.
britannica-1911-elegy:
Elegy, a short poem of grief or loss, is traced from Greek roots in a 1911 Britannica verse entry. The Greek word at its root has a dim sense in the text. Most take it to mean a sad song or a song for the dead. Yet the first Greek elegies that still live sing of war and love, not of death. Callinus of Ephesus is the first such poet with scraps still left.

Tyrtaeus sang war verse in Sparta, and Mimnermus sang of love in the same form. More verse from Theognis lives than from any peer of his age. The form sank for a time as wild song rose in Greek lands. It rose again in the age of Alexandria, with Callimachus at its head. Love stayed its chief theme in that late bloom.
britannica-1911-energy:
Energy, in physical science, is treated at length in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word comes from a Greek term tied to work. It may be defined as accumulated mechanical work, though that work may be only in part available for use. A bent spring has energy, since it can do work as it springs back to its natural form.

A charge of gunpowder has energy, since it can do work when it explodes. A charged Leyden jar has energy, since it can do work in being discharged. The motions of bodies involve energy too, since stopping them would yield work. All kinds of energy are in the end measured in terms of work. The entry shows this with weights raised against the pull of the earth. Doubling the weight, or doubling the height, doubles the work done.
britannica-1911-entomology:
Entomology is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on the science of insects. The hosted text opens with the tail of a logic entry, then gives this article in full. The word joins Greek terms for insects and for discourse. The science deals with the class Hexapoda, part of the Arthropoda. In wide use, the term may also cover spiders and centipedes.

The entry traces the study from old art and scripture to science. Beetles appear in old Egyptian carving, and bees and ants in Hebrew texts. Aristotle first set insects in a class of their own. Later work split into clear lines of study. Some traced body form and growth, some sorted species, and some watched habits. Fossil insects drew fresh interest in later years.
britannica-1911-eschatology:
Eschatology is the church term for the lore of last things, from Greek words for last and for lore. It comes from phrases in the new books that speak of the last day and the last times. In the first church age folk held that the return of Christ was near. That return would close the tale of the world.

The term now spans all that the books teach on life past death and on the end of the world. The entry first scans views of the next life in faiths round the globe. Views range from plain life on, to pay back for deeds done here.
britannica-1911-fejer-gyorgy:
Gyorgy Fejer (1766-1851), Hungarian author, was born on 23 April 1766 at Keszthely in the county of Zala. He studied philosophy at Pest and theology at Pressburg. In 1808 he gained a theology professorship at Pest University, in 1818 became chief director of the educational district of Raab, and in 1824 librarian to the University of Pest. His works, nearly all in Latin or Hungarian, number more than one hundred and eighty.

Fejer's chief work is the Codex diplomaticus Hungariae, issued from 1829 to 1844, a vast gathering of old documents and charters from the year 104 to the end of 1439. Its eleven named tomes run to more than forty volumes, a monument of patient industry that put him in the first rank of Hungarian historians. His last books, on the origin of the Huns and the causes of political revolutions, appeared in 1850. The second, for its liberal views, was suppressed by Austria. He died on 2 July 1851.
britannica-1911-geology:
Geology, in the 1911 Britannica, is one of the longest science articles in the set. The hosted text opens in mid-course, inside a history of early fossil study. That stretch names Lister, Plot and Llwyd in England, Woodward's fossil collection left to Cambridge, and the great Nuremberg picture-book of fossils begun by Knorr and finished by Walch.

From the history of fossils the article moves through the science's growth as a whole. Hutton's name recurs, and stratigraphy, the reading of layered rocks, is a running theme. The treatment is historical as well as technical, tracing how scattered fossil collecting hardened into a science of the earth's crust. Readers should note that the opening of the article is missing from the hosted text; what survives is a long central portion, rich in names, dates and works.
britannica-1911-hagiology:
Hagiology, in the 1911 Britannica, is a study entry on the branch of history that deals with the lives of the saints. As a strict science of testing old texts, it can be dated no earlier than the 17th century. Its roots run far deeper, to the first gatherings of scattered saint texts into sets. The oldest such set, by Eusebius, is lost in full, though traces of it remain.

In the Greek Church the great sets were menologies, lives laid out by month. One by Metaphrastes, from the late 10th century, was read near everywhere. The West had its passionaries and legendaries, drawn from a shared Roman stock plus local saints. From these came the Legenda aurea of Jacobus de Voragine. The entry maps where the raw lives of saints were kept and how scholars test them.
britannica-1911-histology: Histology is a one-line entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It names the science that deals with the fine structure of the tissues of plants and of animals. The word comes from a Greek term for a web or tissue, from the beam of a loom. The entry sends the reader on to the article on cytology for the full treatment. No more than this bare definition is given under this head.
britannica-1911-hydra-mythology:
Hydra is a short myth entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It tells of a huge water snake in Greek legend, born of two old monsters. The beast had nine heads, and the middle head could not be killed. It lived in the marsh land near Argos, by a river and a plane tree.

The entry recounts how the hero Heracles killed the beast as one of his twelve labours. Each cut head grew back as two, so his helper burned each stump with fire. The hero then buried the deathless head under a great rock. The entry also gives two plain readings of the tale, one tied to swamp land and one tied to a siege.
britannica-1911-linus-mythology:
Linus is one of a class of heroic figures in Greek legend, and this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article sets out his story. Like Hyacinthus and Adonis, he is a beautiful youth who loves hunting and rural life. He is the favourite of some god or goddess. Then he perishes suddenly by a terrible death. Yearly rites often kept the religious core of such tales alive.

At Argos the Linus myth kept that character best. Linus was the secret child of Psamathe by the god Apollo. He was exposed, nursed by sheep, and torn in pieces by sheep-dogs. Each year the women of Argos mourned for him and sought to appease Apollo, who had sent a monster against their children. In the Theban version, Linus is a famous musician, inventor of the Linus song, slain by Apollo for daring a contest.
britannica-1911-liturgy:
Liturgy comes from a Greek word that joins the senses of public and work. A liturgist was a public servant in the old tongue. In the strict speech of the Christian Church, liturgy names the order for the rite of the Eucharist. In the Eastern Church, the Greek word is used in that sense and in that sense alone. In lands where English is spoken, though, the word has come to bear a wider sense in common use.

In that wider sense, liturgy can mean any or all of the services of the Church. Those services may be held in books of their own, or bound up in one Book of Common Prayer. In this article, the word is used in the first and strict sense. To make terms and cross notes clear, the article gives a table of the chief parts of a liturgy.
britannica-1911-lung-mythology: Lung, in a short 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry, is one of the four symbolical creatures of Chinese legend. The entry describes it as a dragon with a scaly snake-like body, long claws, and horns. Its face is bristly and its back is armed with spikes. First shown with three claws, it became a five-clawed beast as the official dragon of the ruling house. Its form was worked into the state robes of the emperor of China, and custom linked it with the history and fortunes of that house.
britannica-1911-martyrology:
Martyrology is a church article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about the lists of martyrs and saints kept in the order of their feast days. That is the settled sense of the word in the Latin Church; the Greek Church's nearest match is the Synaxarium. The article sorts the lists by form: simple martyrologies give names only, while historical ones add tales or life details.

The great old book of the field is the compilation falsely laid to St Jerome, which in its present shape goes back to the end of the sixth century. The text has come down in a sorry state, with names twisted, doubled, or misplaced. Of the historical lists the most famed is that of Usuard, about 875, on which the Roman martyrology rests.
britannica-1911-metallurgy:
Metallurgy, the art of taking metals from their ores by trade methods, is laid out in a long entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Work done in a lab does not count under the term here. A table ranks the metals by weight in trade. It pairs iron, copper, silver, gold, lead, zinc, and tin with the kinds of ore each one comes from.

Pure masses of ore are rare in mines. Most ore comes out mixed with waste rock called gangue. Since ore tends to weigh more than the waste, that gap helps sort and clean it. The text walks through this first stage before the metal is freed. It gives readers a sound base for the steps that follow.
britannica-1911-narcissus-mythology:
Narcissus, in Greek tale, is the son of a river god and a nymph, and the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica tells his tale in brief. He was marked out for his great beauty. A seer told his mother a hard fate for the boy. He would live long if he never saw his own face.

His cold spurn of the love of the nymph Echo drew the wrath of the gods on him. He fell in love with his own face in the still pool of a spring. There he pined away. The flower that bears his name sprang up on the spot where he died. A Greek road writer gives a soft twist to the tale. In his form the youth gazed to call back the face of a dead twin sister, his twin in looks.
britannica-1911-ontology:
Ontology is a thought article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a branch of the study of truth. The branch deals with the nature of being, or reality in the abstract. The term was shaped from Greek roots for being and for science.

The article traces the line of the thought through great names. Plato used kindred terms for the full reality of his ideas. Aristotle set a first science of being ahead of the rest. The word took its fixed sense in the work of Wolff in later times. He split the study of truth into parts by their objects. In the modern view, the study of knowing comes first. The piece closes by noting that the two studies cannot in the end be pulled apart.
britannica-1911-orgy:
Orgy is the subject of a rites entry in the 1911 Britannica. The hosted text first gives a short note on a logic term. It then turns to orgy as its true topic. The word came through French from Latin and Greek roots. At first it named secret rites of worship. Those rites were tied most of all to Dionysus. Rites for that god were held in winter hills.

Only women took part in those Thracian rites. They wore fawn skins with hair loose and wild. They swung staffs and beat cymbals as they danced. They worked themselves up to a mad state of zeal. The most holy rites took place at night. Torch light lit the acts in the dark hills. A bull that stood for the god was torn apart. The entry ties that act to the myth of the god.
britannica-1911-pan-mythology:
Pan is a god of shepherds, flocks, and forests in Greek myth, as a 1911 Britannica entry tells. His name points to pasturing, and his parentage is given two ways in old tales. Homer and Hesiod never name him, yet a Homeric hymn gives his life in verse. He was born with horns, a goat beard, goat feet, and a tail.

Hair covered his body, and his mother fled at the sight of the child. Hermes bore him to Olympus, where the gods took him as a favourite. Dionysus loved him most among that bright company of heaven. His life matched the old goatherds, wild, musical, and free on the hills.
britannica-1911-pharmacology:
Pharmacology is a term whose scope is weighed in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word joins Greek roots for a drug and for discourse. Writers differ much on how wide a field it should cover. One German author takes in the origin, nature, and uses of drugs entire.

French and Italian usage narrows the term to describing medicines and their making. English usage, backed by most German writers, settles the matter otherwise. There the word means the study of how chemical substances act on living things. The range runs from bacteria up to man himself, foods set aside. One aim is sound knowledge of remedies for treating disease. Another is the finding of new or better remedies for that work. The article notes a rival term, pharmaco-dynamics, judged more correct in form. It never won wide use, and the older word stands.
britannica-1911-pleiades-mythology:
Pleiades, in Greek myth, are the seven daughters of Atlas and Pleione, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets out. They were sisters of the Hyades in the old tales. In one account their grief at the death of their sisters, or at the pain of their father, led to their change into stars. In an other, they met the hunter Orion in Boeotia with their mother.

The sight of the group fired the passion of Orion at that meeting. He chased them through the woods for five years in the tale. Zeus then lifted them all, mother, daughters, Orion, and his dog, into the sky. The Pleiades rose in mid May and set at the end of October in the Greek year. That link with spring and autumn is held to explain the legend in full.
britannica-1911-possession-psychology:
Possession, as a term of law, is the subject of the hosted text for this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. The text deals with what it means in law to hold land or goods, and what rights flow from that hold. In English law, it says, possession gives much the same rights as in Roman law. It can found a title, and it puts the burden of proof on the person who claims against the holder.

The text goes on to compare the two systems of law in detail. Roman law was more strict on the need for a just title or colour of right. English law gives some rights to those who hold through others, such as in pledge. Possession also shapes how estates in land are split, and it can serve as first proof of seisin against a wrongdoer.
britannica-1911-python-mythology:
Python, in Greek mythology, was a huge serpent and son of Gaea. Its myth entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Men said the beast was born from mud left after the flood of Deucalion. Its lair was a cavern near Mount Parnassus in Greece.

Four days after its birth, Apollo slew Python, Apollodorus tells us here. Apollo took the name Pythius from that famed early deed of his. One writer Ephorus held Python was a brigand near Delphi instead. The entry reads the serpent as foul vapours from still lakes. Sun shafts of Apollo, in that view, scatter those vapours away.
britannica-1911-sill-geology:
Sill, in rock lore, names a flat sheet of fire rock set deep in the earth in this 1911 Britannica entry. Such a sheet spreads wide in reach when set by its depth. The great Whin Sill of north east England sets the type for the form. Its name whin is a folk word for hard dark rock in those parts. The sheet is a mass of dark hard stone of the basalt kin.

Its outcrop runs some eighty miles in a great curve to the sea. In spots it stands out as a bold crag ridge past soft stone. Falls leap where streams cross its hard lip in the dales. Its depth runs from twenty to one hundred fifty feet in range. Small kin sheets in Scots coal fields share its late fire age.
britannica-1911-strategy:
Strategy, in its root sense the art of the leader or general, is the subject of an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word entered European writing on war near the start of the eighteenth century. At that time war had settled into set routine, and armies were near equal in strength. A small trick or ruse could tip the scale between them.

For a time the word thus clung to the idea of a stratagem or clever trick. In the Napoleonic period that view faded, and the root sense came back to the fore. Strategy became the practice of the art of war by the agent of a supreme government. Moltke put it as fitting the means at a general's disposal to the aim in view. The entry stresses that the commander answers for how he uses those means, not for the means themselves.
britannica-1911-veins-geology:
Veins, in geology, are masses of rock that fill cracks in other rocks, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article explains. They fall into three groups: veins of igneous rock, of settled rock, and of minerals laid down by water or gases. Igneous veins are much like dikes, though dikes run straighter and farther while veins are broken and short.

Where granite pushes into older rocks it throws out swarms of dikes, until no line can be drawn where solid granite ends. Great buried masses grew by inflow upon inflow, the later rock often less basic than the first, which makes the veining stand out. In banded gneisses such veining is nearly universal, the new threads running with the grain or across it. Some rocks are so stuffed with granite threads that their whole look and make-up change.
britannica-1911-zoology:
Zoology is a science article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about the branch of biology that deals with animals. The word joins Greek terms for a living thing and for theory. Botany is its twin branch, for plants. The history of the field opens the entry.

The article speaks of the sad charm in early man's wonder at tales of strange beasts from far lands and deep seas. Such tales fill the old Physiologus and the works of Albertus Magnus. That age of fable gave way to an age of collectors and travellers. Their real specimens, brought home alive or preserved, proved some wild stories true. Proof became a habit, and close watching of things replaced the mere heaping up of reports. The entry sets that shift at the root of the modern science.
bulfinch-s-mythology:
Thomas Bulfinch's Mythology gathers his three books in one complete volume. The Age of Fable retells the myths of Greece, Rome, and the north for general readers. The Age of Chivalry follows King Arthur and the knights of romance. Legends of Charlemagne completes the set with the paladins of France.

The publishers' preface ranks The Age of Fable with Pilgrim's Progress and Robinson Crusoe among books everyone must know. Bulfinch, a Boston bank accountant born in 1796, wrote in his leisure from Harvard studies. He meant mythology as a key to literature and art, not as scholarship. Story follows story, plainly told and lightly moralized. For generations of English-speaking children this was the door into Olympus and Camelot. Its versions still shape how the old tales are remembered, quoted, and retold.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abraham-in-li:
Abraham holds a special place in Christian liturgy, and this entry traces his name through the prayers and rites of East and West. Of all Old Testament names used in worship, Abel, Melchisedech, and Abraham gain prominence through their link with sacrifice. That link matters above all in the Roman rite's Canon of the Mass. In the Litany for the Dying only two Old Testament names appear, Abel and Abraham, and Abraham occurs so often that his position stands out.

The entry works through his present uses in the Roman liturgy, from the Martyrology entry for 9 October to the commendation of a departing soul. It calls him patriarch and father of all believers. It also looks back to his name in sacred history and early Christian prayer. Its use even in pagan magical formulas, as Origen testifies, shows how widely the patriarch's name travelled.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-african-litur:
The African Liturgy was in use not only in old Roman Africa, with Carthage as capital, but also in Numidia and Mauretania, across northern Africa from Egypt's borders west to the Atlantic. Christianity entered proconsular Africa late in the second century, probably through missionaries from Rome, and spread rapidly through the other provinces. The liturgy's language was Latin, modified by many Africanisms.

Probably the oldest Latin liturgy, it was in use long before Rome changed her official language from Greek to Latin. Studying it may therefore trace the origin and growth of different rites and show one rite's influence on another. Since the African church always depended on Rome and stayed devoted to St. Peter's see, liturgical questions were surely raised and customs possibly adopted each way. Later the African liturgy seems to have influenced Mozarabic and Gallican rites.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-agnus-dei-in-:
Agnus Dei in liturgy is the thrice-recited Mass formula of the priest in the Roman rite, except on Good Friday and Holy Saturday. It comes toward the Canon's end, after the prayer Haec commixtio. Having finished that prayer, the priest lays the pall over the chalice, genuflects, rises, and inclines his head profoundly toward the altar. Then he says aloud: Agnus Dei, qui tollis peccata mundi, miserere nobis.

In English: Lamb of God, who takest away the sins of the world, have mercy on us. He repeats the formula unchanged, then a third time substitutes dona nobis pacem, grant us peace, striking his breast thrice. In Requiem Masses the formula instead asks dona eis requiem, grant them rest, and dona eis requiem sempiternam, grant them eternal rest, and the priest does not strike his breast.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-in-litu:
In the New Law the altar is the Eucharistic Sacrifice's table, and Mass is never celebrated without an altar or at least an altar stone. Only two exceptions appear in church history: St. Lucian celebrating on his breast in prison in 312, and Theodore of Tyre on his deacons' hands. In ancient basilicas the priest faced the people, the apse holding the altar at the end opposite the entrance.

Early altars were probably wood, like Christ's Last Supper table, a Roman wooden table surviving at the Lateran. A fixed altar joins table, support, and sepulchre, the table a single stone slab cemented to its support. A portable altar is a consecrated stone holding host and chalice base. Primitive forms included the arcosolium, a marble slab over a martyr's grave niche in the catacombs.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-analogy:
Analogy, a term from philosophy, names both a property of things and a way of reasoning. It is treated in four parts: science, scholastic thought, God, and the mysteries of faith. As a property it means likeness mixed with difference. The likeness may live only in the mind, as between sunlight and the light of the mind. It may also rest on real shared traits, as with organs serving the same use in different creatures.

As reasoning, it argues from known likenesses to further ones. Franklin moved by this path from lightning to electricity, and Cuvier rebuilt whole animals from single bones. Scholastic writers refined it into proportion and proportionality, using health as their model, since food, medicine, and a face can all be called healthy for different reasons. Applied to God, it strips limits from what it finds in creatures, then lifts the perfections that remain higher.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anatole-de-be:
A martyr of the French Commune, Anatole de Bengy was born at Bourges on 19 September 1824 and died in Paris on 26 May 1871. After nine years at the Jesuit college of Brugelette he entered the Society of Jesus. He served as chaplain to French troops in the Crimean War, then gave himself to college work until 1870.

When the Franco-Prussian War broke out he again became a chaplain, serving the sick and wounded through the siege of Paris. After the war he returned to teach at Sainte-Genevieve. On 3 April National Guards seized the school and held its Jesuits as hostages of the Commune. De Bengy cheered his companions through the wait for death. On 26 May he was led with two Jesuit companions and some forty other victims to the court at Rue Haxo. There he died joyfully amid the shouts of the Communards.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antiochene-li:
The Antioch liturgy family begins with the Apostolic Constitutions, then Greek and Syrian St. James, and other Syrian Anaphoras. The line continues to the Byzantine Rite, Basil's older and Chrysostom's shorter liturgies, and through it to Armenian use. These no longer concern Antioch. The Apostolic Constitutions liturgy is the oldest known complete liturgy form. It is the Antiochene line's first member. The Constitutions are eight books ascribed to St. Clement of Rome. The first six books are an interpolated Didascalia edition.

The Constitutions liturgy moves from Institution words to Anamimnesis, remembrance of suffering, death, resurrection, ascension, and second coming. Then Epiklesis invokes the Spirit to change bread and cup, and a great Intercession follows. The developed St. James liturgy adds Diptychs, anti-Nestorian hymns to Our Lady, the Lord's Prayer, and a Communion where the deacon says only Approach in the fear of the Lord.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antiphon-in-g:
Antiphons appear throughout the Greek Liturgy: in the Office, at Mass, at Vespers, and at every canonical Hour. Almost every liturgical function gives them a set place. In antiphonal psalmody, soloists and choir take turns rendering a psalm. Alternate singing entered liturgical worship about the fourth century, after use only in secular gatherings until then.

That does not mean antiphonal chanting was new in the fourth century: the Synagogue already used it, and the Church would hardly have waited so long to take it up. What was new was a more ornate melody. Choir-rendered strophes in antiphon form explain why alternate psalmody is called antiphonal. Hymn writers found endless material in those strophes, so psalm verses slowly gave way to added strophes. Some psalms or psalm groups shrank in this way to three or four verses, and sometimes to a single verse.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apostle-in-li: Apostle, in liturgy, is the name the Greek church gives to the Epistle, or letter reading, of the Divine Liturgy. It is always of apostolic origin and never, as sometimes in the Roman rite, sourced from the Old Testament writings. It is also the book holding the Epistles for each Sunday and feast of the year, from which the reader reads the Epistle of the day. As printed at Constantinople, Athens, and Rome, it adds the antiphons and prokeimena, or introductory verses, for the days of the Greek church year.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-archaeology:
Archaeology, in this entry, means the official pontifical board founded in the mid-nineteenth century to promote and direct digs in the Roman catacombs and other sites of Christian antiquarian interest. It also safeguards objects found there. Its spur was Giovanni Battista De Rossi, pupil of the archaeologist Father Marchi, who had begun investigating underground Rome with results that promised rich reward.

In a vineyard plot on the Appian Way in 1849 De Rossi found a marble fragment reading in part NELIVS MARTYR, which he recognized as part of Pope Cornelius's tomb inscription. Cornelius, martyred in 253, lay in St. Callixtus's catacomb on the Appian Way, and De Rossi argued the vineyard overlay that catacomb. He urged Pius IX to buy the vineyard for digging, and the pope, hearing the young enthusiast, answered that these were but the dreams of an archaeologist.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ascetical-the:
Ascetical theology, as a branch of theology, is the scientific exposition of Christian asceticism. Asceticism, from Greek askesis, literally means polishing, smoothing, or refining. Greeks used the word for athletes' exercises, by which dormant bodily powers were developed and the body trained to full natural beauty. They aimed at the laurel wreath given to victors in public games.

Christian life, Christ assures us, is a struggle for the kingdom of heaven. Paul, trained in Greek fashion, pictures that spiritual battle with the Greek pentathlon, the five contests, in 1 Corinthians 9:24. Exercises in this combat develop moral stamina, aiming at Christian perfection. The long article expounds that training: its principles, its stages, and its place beside dogmatic and moral theology in the science of the spiritual life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-assemblies-of:
The Assemblies of the French Clergy were five-yearly representative meetings of France's clergy to apportion financial burdens kings laid on the church, and incidentally for other church purposes. They had a financial origin, to which, the article argues, the rise of all deliberative assemblies may be traced. Long before them, the state had imposed on the church its share of public expenses.

French kings, powerful, needy, and at times unscrupulous, could hardly see a wealthy body steadily extending its possessions without drawing on its coffers, or if need be pillaging them. During the Middle Ages Crusades brought frequent levies on church property, and the Saladin Tithe began that pattern. The long article follows assemblies from tax bargaining to a forum where clergy debated money, discipline, and the crown's claims.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-astrology:
Astrology is the supposed science fixing the stars' influence, above all the five older planets, on human fate, called judicial or mundane astrology, or on weather changes, called natural astrology. It works by fixed rules depending on the stars' controlling positions at the time in question. Judicial astrology, the more important branch of this occult art, based predictions on the planets' places in the twelve houses at a person's birth moment.

The calculations settling those positions meant casting the horoscope, or diagram of the heavens, at nativity. Starting from the point rising at birth, the celestial equator was divided into a dozen equal parts, six above and six beneath the horizon. Circles were drawn through those points and the horizon and meridian crossings. The long article then explains houses, aspects, and the church's judgment on a practice that claimed the stars ruled human lives.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-benefit-of-cl:
Benefit of clergy, the medieval English exemption of clergy from secular courts, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. In Saxon days bishops sat beside sheriffs in local courts, but after the Norman Conquest church courts stood apart from civil ones. The privilege covered all who were tonsured, with shaved crown, and wore clerical dress, including monks and nuns.

Gratian's canon law sums the rule: a cleric was not to be brought before public courts in civil or criminal cases. The entry follows the privilege through its widening, its abuses, and its slow narrowing by English kings. It reads as a compact history of church and crown competing for jurisdiction.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-biblical-chro:
Biblical chronology, the dating of Bible events, receives a very long entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. It asks whether the Bible holds a chronology at all, how far its writers aimed at exact dates or round numbers, and how far copyists' errors corrupted its figures. Relations with neighbouring peoples' chronologies form the fourth question.

No single era anchored early Bible history, unlike Rome's founding or the later Seleucid era from 312 BC. The entry works in sections from creation and the Flood through Abraham, Exodus, kings, and exile, weighing rival systems. It is a sober admission that Bible dates often resist a single timeline.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-biology:
Biology, the science of life and living things, receives a long survey in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. From the Greek words for life and account, it studies structure, origin, growth, function, and surroundings of plants and animals, by observation and experiment. Zoology covers animals, botany covers plants, and anthropology covers humankind's body.

Morphology, the study of form, splits into anatomy of gross structure, histology of tissues, and cytology of cells, the ultimate units of life. Classification, physiology, and development follow. The entry is a map of a young science, written before genetics reshaped it, but clear on its branches.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-celibacy-of-t:
Celibacy is the giving up of marriage, promised implicitly or explicitly for the sake of perfect chastity, by all who receive Orders in any higher grade. Its character is understood differently in the Eastern and Western Churches. In the West, the bishop warns candidates at ordination of the burden they take on. He tells them they are still free to turn back to the world.

But once they receive the order, they must persevere in God's service and chastity. By stepping forward despite the warning, the candidate binds himself equivalently by a vow of chastity and can no longer contract a valid marriage. The long article traces the history of clerical celibacy in two periods, its course in England, and its present position. It also covers the law in the Oriental Churches, closing with an 1898 Coptic synod at Alexandria requiring celibacy of candidates for higher orders.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christian-arc:
An entry on Christian archaeology, the study of ancient Christian monuments as a source for early Christian life. The historian has two sources: literary remains and material monuments, from tomb inscriptions, paintings, and sculptures to churches and small crafted objects. Its aim is to learn the manners and customs of the first Christians from what they made and left behind.

Authorities such as De Rossi and Le Blant close Christian antiquity about the death of Gregory the Great in 604. In Gaul and Germany monuments kept an ancient character a century longer. Scientific study began with the Augustinian Onofrio Panvinio in 1554 and 1568, and the chance discovery of a Christian cemetery on the Via Salaria in 1578 opened the field. The entry surveys inscriptions, frescoes, mosaics, basilicas, and minor arts, including textiles, vessels, coins, and miniatures.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christology:
An entry on Christology, the part of theology that deals with Our Lord Jesus Christ. In full it covers both His person and His works, but this article limits itself to His person. The historian's and Old Testament scholar's shares go to the articles on Jesus Christ and the Messiah. Its subject is the person of Christ as the New Testament and Christian tradition present Him.

That person is the Second Person of the Trinity, the Son or Word of the Father, incarnate by the Holy Ghost of the Virgin Mary and made man. Foretold in the Old Testament and fully revealed in the New, these mysteries are studied under three aspects: Old Testament, New Testament, and Christian tradition. The Old Testament section notes how Christ and the apostles appealed to messianic prophecies, and how the Fathers prepared a deeper reading of their historical sweep.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-commemoration:
Patrick Morrisroe's entry defines a commemoration in liturgy as part of an Office or Mass said for a feast or day when the whole cannot be said. Two Offices may fall on one day, and rubrics may bar moving one to another day. Then the lesser is kept in part, by way of commemoration. Offices carry grades of rank, such as doubles and semi-doubles, fixed at their founding. Rank mainly settles which Office wins when they clash.

At Mass a commemoration means saying the collect, Secret, and Post-Communion proper to the feast remembered. In the Office, commemorations fall at Lauds and Vespers, with antiphons, versicles, and responses of the Benedictus and Magnificat, plus an oremus. Special commemorations differ from common ones, which belong to Offices of lower rite. When two Offices meet, the clash is called occurrence, or concurrence at Vespers, and rank fixes their order.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-convocation-o:
Edward Myers's entry defines Convocation, the Church of England's name for what resembles a provincial synod yet differs widely. Canterbury and York each possess one, Canterbury's the more important. Its outward form's history runs on, bound up with English history. Power and freedom vanished at the Reformation, though the body, long a mere form, now voices priestly views. It exercises influence, but holds no power, Crown power remaining supreme.

Its history divides into five periods: before 1295; 1295 to the Reformation; the Reformation period; the post-Reformation period; and modern times. Before 1295 synods regulated discipline. After 1295 beneficed clergy sat in Parliament, and Convocation's link to these men stays obscure. Its Houses split in time, not on Parliament's model. The Act of Submission cost its freedom and powers. Nineteenth-century churchmen revived its use, and the Crown may submit business.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cosmology:
Cosmology, from Greek words for world and knowledge, names the philosophical science of the material universe. Once broad enough to cover plants, animals, and humanity, the field has narrowed to the world studied apart from the natural sciences. Physics and biology chase proximate causes; cosmology asks after deeper ones.

Three questions organise the entry: the first cause of the world, its constituent causes, and its final purpose. Monism, emanation, and creation face off on origins, while mechanism, dynamism, and the Scholastic hylomorphism debate what matter is made of. Geology, the author notes, always stops at a fact still calling for explanation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-demonology:
A wide survey of beliefs about demons across many peoples and ages. Assyrian and Akkadian systems come first, then Iranian, Jewish, early Christian, and medieval and modern forms. True Catholic teaching on fallen angels is set apart from the false and risky systems that fill most of the literature.

Cuneiform records show how old such beliefs are, while Jewish Scripture keeps demon lore spare beside Persian and Assyrian abundance. Early Christian writers faced a crowded field of rival doctrines, and later ages kept borrowing from one system to another. Shared threads run through them all, from belief in evil spirits to modern spiritism, and the closing pages weigh rival explanations for that spread.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-divorce-in-mo:
Divorce in moral theology takes up the word where the civil article leaves it. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry explains that pagan Rome used divorce for the mutual parting of spouses. The word alone does not say whether the marriage bond itself was broken. Church law therefore keeps the word neutral and splits it into two kinds.

Absolute divorce dissolves the bond itself, while limited divorce leaves the bond whole and ends only common life. Limited divorce may mean parting from bed and board, or parting of dwelling as well. The entry then sets out the moral teaching in full, with Jewish divorce law and the Christian law of marriage treated side by side.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dogmatic-theo:
Dogmatic theology treats the theoretical truths of faith about God and his works, while moral theology treats the practical truths of conduct. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry notes that apologetics was once called general dogmatic theology, though it now stands as its own science and doorway to the field. The article takes up first the basic questions of the science, then its history.

That history follows the acumen and tireless labor of theologians from the fathers through the schoolmen to modern writers. It names the great handbooks, from Pohle to Hettinger, and the aids to clerical study. For students of theology, it is both a definition of the field and a map of its growth across the centuries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-doxology:
A doxology is a short verse praising God, most often opening with the Greek word for glory. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry traces the habit of closing a rite or hymn with such a formula to the synagogue. Saint Paul uses doxologies constantly in his letters, and the earliest Christian forms address God the Father alone, or the Father through the Son, or with the Holy Spirit. The baptismal form named the three persons in parallel order.

In the fourth century the wording became a weapon against Arian teaching, since heretics leaned on the little prepositions through, in, and with. Basil defended the Church's phrasing, and the entry follows the doxology from synagogue to Mass. It closes with liturgists from Bona to Thalhofer who charted its growth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-epistemology:
Epistemology is the branch of philosophy concerned with the value of human knowledge, from the Greek words for knowledge and discourse. The name is recent, but since Ferrier's Institutes of Metaphysics in 1854 it has come into common use, replacing terms such as applied logic, critical logic, and initial philosophy. Latin textbooks and the Louvain school call the same field criteriology.

Its exact province is still unsettled, since the Greek word for knowledge bears two senses. In the wider sense epistemology is the theory of the origin, nature, and limits of knowledge, the usual English meaning, matching the German theory of knowing. In the narrower sense it is the philosophy of the sciences: a critical study of each science's principles, hypotheses, and results, judging their logical origin, value, and objective import. Italian and French usage agrees with the narrower sense. This entry follows the wider, English meaning.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eschatology:
Eschatology is the branch of systematic theology dealing with the doctrines of the last things, ta eschata. The Greek title is recent, but it has largely replaced the Latin De Novissimis. Other doctrines in this field are treated under their own titles, so this article merely surveys the whole field. It indicates eschatology's place in religion and compares its content across religions, illustrating the superiority of Christian teaching.

A distinction is made between the eschatology of the individual and that of the race and universe. The former, starting from personal immortality, seeks the fate of individual souls and how far the future depends on the present life. The latter deals with the resurrection and general judgment, and with the signs preceding those events. Both aspects belong to the full concept, but only Christian teaching gives both due recognition.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-general-chron:
General Chronology, the science of fixing dates in the stream of time, is history's answer to geography's latitude and longitude. Its first need is an era, a fixed point from which all other years take their distance. The article treats the systems that matter for Christian history, from the Christian era itself to regnal years, indictions, and the reform of the calendar.

Dionysius Exiguus, a Scythian monk at Rome, framed the Christian era about 527, counting from Rome's year 753 as the birth year of Christ, with no year zero between BC and AD. Italy took it first, England early through Roman missionaries, Gaul in the eighth century, and Europe at large only after 1000. Greek Olympiads, the Julian period, and other eras fill out the survey.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gospel-in-the:
The Gospel in the Liturgy is an article on the public reading of Scripture in worship, inherited from the synagogue service. Before the bread and wine were brought for offering, the Liturgy of the Catechumens offered prayers, litanies, hymns, and readings to instruct the people. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows the Gospel's rise to the crown of the readings.

Books were rare and few could read. What early Christians knew of the Bible, Paul's theology, and the Lord's life came from lessons heard in church and the homilies that explained them. Justin Martyr, who died about 167, describes Sunday readings of the Apostles' memoirs or the Prophets, read as long as time allowed, then exhortation by the president. Common practice read first the Prophecy, then the Epistle, and last the Gospel, as fulfillment of all the rest.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-heortology: Heortology, from the Greek words for festival and discourse, is the science of sacred festivals. It treats their origin, significance, and historical development in relation to epochs and incidents of the Christian year. Though the word etymologically covers feasts in general, the entry uses it specifically for the study of Christian festivals and their meaning.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-history-of-do:
This vast article traces how Catholic dogmatic theology grew, not by single nations or men, but by the combined efforts of all nations and theologians of every century. Like the church itself, theology must stay international, the entry insists, and no national stamp fits its character. Its history falls into three periods: patristic, medieval, and modern.

The patristic age, about AD 100 to 800, honoured the great Fathers as the church's principal theologians, praised for purity of faith, holiness of life, and fullness of wisdom. Tertullian and Origen strayed on some points, and even Cyprian and Gregory of Nyssa erred on single questions. Medieval schools then carried the work forward through fierce debates, and modern theology inherited both their gains and their divisions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hymnody-and-h:
Hymnody, from the Greek for hymn song, covers hymnal verse or religious lyric, including both hymn-singer and hymn-poet. Hymnology is the science of hymnody: the historical, philological, and aesthetic study of hymns and hymn writers. Hymnology is still recent in origin, and the vast Latin hymn material long lay buried in Europe's library manuscripts.

Interest in spreading knowledge and love of hymns, especially Latin hymns, dates to the twelfth century, and research quickened in England, France, and Germany from the mid-nineteenth century. Yet a German encyclopedia judged that research into Latin church poetry had made little progress despite nineteenth-century studies. Even the compilations of Neale, Mone, and Daniel, once thought fairly complete, proved only a beginning.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lessons-in-th:
Lessons in the Liturgy, apart from the Gospel, traces Bible, Martyrs' Acts, and Fathers' lessons as a key part of worship in every rite from the start.  The Christian synaxis copied the synagogue service: lessons, psalm-singing, homilies, and prayers. Christians read their own Scriptures too: Gospels and Apostles' letters.

St. Paul bids the Thessalonians have his letter read to all the brethren. He tells the Colossians to exchange letters with Laodicea for reading. The common view that Paul's Gospel through all the churches meant Luke's Gospel read in assemblies shows the same.  Tertullian says Rome joined Law and Prophets with Gospels and Apostolic letters in public reading. At first Acts of Martyrs, letters, homilies of leading bishops, and other edifying writings were also read aloud.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-liturgy:
Liturgy, from a Greek word for public duty, is the Church's official public worship, set against private prayer. At Athens rich citizens bore a leitourgia at their own cost, funding choruses, banquets, or warships, and the Septuagint took the word for temple service.

Christians kept the religious sense, and the entry uses it to compare all the great rites: Alexandrine, Ambrosian, Antiochene, Celtic, Gallican, Mozarabic, Sarum, Syrian, and more. It asks how fixed forms grew out of free prayer in the early Church, and how sister rites split, borrowed, and kept a family likeness across East and West.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-martyrology:
A martyrology is a list of martyrs and saints set out by feast day, that is, by calendar. Since martyr commemorations began, each church kept its own list, and local lists grew by borrowing neighbours' names. When the martyr era closed, those famed for holy life and ascetic practice joined the lists. Rome's mid-fourth-century martyrology, or ferial, survives in two lists, Depositio martyrum and Depositio episcoporum, usually found united elsewhere.

The Hieronymian Martyrology and its kin show hasty work, while historical martyrologies link to great Greek synaxaries, a key counterpart. Critical study stays hard, given the sheer mix of elements involved. For long, study of the Hieronymian text yielded few results.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mental-pathol:
Mental pathology is surveyed under five heads. They are where mental powers sit in the brain, what disturbs them, the kinds of insanity, freedom of the will and responsibility, and pathological changes in brain structure. The kinds alone run to fourteen. They are melancholia and mania, general paresis, juvenile insanity, senile dementia, chronic delusion, alcoholic disease, epileptic psychosis, hysterical psychosis, imbecility, compulsive ideas, menstrual psychosis, impulsive psychosis, and sexual psychopathy.

On localization, the cerebral cortex, the thin coat over the brain's whole surface, holds areas linked by long nerve tracts to sense organs, skin, and muscles. These form the Projection System. Other areas, tied to no outer world but joined closely to each other and to the projection areas, form the Association System. In the first, elementary functions sit in sharp centres for limb movements, taste, hearing, sight, and more.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-moral-theolog:
Moral theology is the branch of theology that studies how human beings should act in light of God's revelation. It stands apart from dogmatic theology, which studies what is to be believed. Theology itself divides into natural theology, what reason alone can reach about God, and supernatural theology, the science of God and divine things known through revelation. That science includes his works of salvation and our guidance toward him.

Faith gives believers these truths in outline, but science demands they be deepened, defended by reasons and arranged in order. Moral theology does that work for conduct. The entry surveys its history from Scripture and the Fathers through Aquinas and later schools. It covers its sources in law, conscience and virtue, and its method for judging concrete acts, sins and duties.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mystical-theo:
