Mystical theology is the science of acts, experiences and states of the soul that human effort cannot produce, even with the ordinary aid of divine grace. It covers extraordinary prayer, higher contemplation in all its varieties and grades, private revelations, visions, and the union growing from these between God and the soul, known as the mystical union.

As the science of all that is extraordinary between Divinity and the human spirit, it complements ascetical theology, which treats Christian perfection gained by practising virtue and observing the counsels. Its contents are doctrinal as well as experimental. It records the experiences of mystically favoured souls and lays down rules for their guidance, drawn from Scripture, the Fathers and theologian-mystics. Its precepts serve directors of souls, guarding them from error while easing their advance, and it notes false systems such as Quietism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ontology:
Ontology, from Greek words for being and science, is the first branch of metaphysics, the philosophy of being itself. Aristotle called it first philosophy, theology, and wisdom, Clauberg used ontology in its literal sense, and Wolff fixed it as general metaphysics against cosmology, psychology, and theodicy.

Its matter runs from the concept of being in widest range, through essence and existence, act and potency, to principles like contradiction and identity. Then come properties as wide as being itself: unity, truth, and goodness, with order and beauty beside them, and the split of being into finite and infinite.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-palaeontology:
Palaeontology, the science of fossils, treats extinct animals and plants of long ago. It covers their features, sorting, life and habits, spread across the earth, and order in time. It also draws lessons from them for the history of living things and of the earth itself. It stands close to geology, botany, zoology, comparative anatomy, and embryology, which serve it as helper sciences.

Fossil plants form palaeophytology, fossil animals palaeozoology. Even in antiquity, sea fossils inland led thinkers like Xenophanes, Strabo, and Seneca to infer a changed layout of sea and land. Medieval writers mostly called fossils sports of earth's shaping power. Later pages trace the science's rise, its use in dating rock layers, and its bearing on descent theory, where fossil series of small steps are weighed against gaps in the record.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pastoral-theo:
Pastoral theology treats the care of souls as a science, and this entry defines it, relates it to other theological sciences, and traces its history, sources, and contents. It belongs to practical theology. Every branch of theology aims to make priests ministers of Christ and dispensers of God's mysteries. Pastoral theology takes the findings of dogmatic, moral, juridical, ascetical, liturgical, and exegetical study, and applies them to priestly ministry.

Dogmatic theology sets out the Church as keeper of revealed truth, and pastoral theology teaches the priest his share in handing it down. Moral theology states God's and the Church's laws, means of grace, and hindrances, and pastoral theology shows their bearing on a priest's life, alone and among his people. Canon law gathers church laws, and pastoral theology applies them, with later pages on preaching, catechism, confession, and sick calls. Its lessons reach the priest in pulpit, confessional, and sickroom.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-patrology:
Patrology is the study of the Fathers' writings, more often called patristics or patristic study in England. Some German writers split the field. Fessler defines patrology as the science that equips readers to use the Fathers. It weighs their authority, tests of genuineness, difficulties, and rules of use. Patristics, by contrast, gathers all on faith, morals, or discipline from their writings. Literary history, a third science, tells the Fathers' lives and works.

Those distinctions are little observed and seem needless, since they are only facets of patristic study within fundamental theology, positive theology, and literary history. Patrology also takes its name from Migne's great collections, the Latin Patrology in 221 volumes and the Greek in 161. Bardenhewer's handbook, translated by Shahan, stands as the most serviceable guide of its kind.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pax-in-the-li:
Pax vobis, or vobiscum, is a liturgical greeting of Scriptural origin, like Dominus vobiscum. The Gospels give may your peace come, may your peace return to you, peace to this house, and peace to you. Grace and peace opens epistles of Saint Paul and Saint Peter, and Saint John's letters and the Apocalypse. Our Lord and the Apostles quoted it from the Old Testament, and it survived in liturgy and inscriptions as a memorial of apostolic times.

Like Dominus vobiscum, bishops first used it in liturgy, as Pax vobis, greeting the faithful at Mass's start before the Collect. When Confiteor, Introit, and Gloria were later added, Pax vobis or Dominus vobiscum stayed. Now bishops and prelates alone use Pax vobis at the first Collect, priests using Dominus vobiscum. Hence Dominus vobiscum became the usual lead-in to orations and most prayers, while Greeks kept Pax omnibus or Pax vobiscum.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-psychology:
Psychology, from the Greek words for soul and study, is the science of the soul and its workings. This long encyclopedia entry notes a shift in the word's use: over the past century it has come to mean the science of mental phenomena, the processes and states of human consciousness. Research has split into distinct fields, each claiming the rank of a separate science. The term itself appeared near the end of the sixteenth century, in Goclenius in 1590 and Casmann's work of 1594.

Higher mental life poses the entry's central problem. Explaining the loftier products of consciousness seems impossible without some metaphysical view of the mind and its link to reality. Dewey's warning is quoted: views about the mind's nature show on almost every page. A neo-Scholastic bibliography, with Baldwin's dictionary and Eisler's lexicon, closes a survey that maps a young science still arguing about its own foundations.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-scriptural-tr:
Scriptural tropology is the theory and practice of reading the figurative meaning of Holy Writ. The literal meaning, the meaning God intended the words to carry, may itself be figurative or plain. In the Song of Songs, for instance, the inspired meaning is always figurative. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia distinguishes two layers of inspired sense.

The typical meaning is the inspired meaning of words about Old Testament persons, things, and actions that serve as types, or foreshadowings, of New Testament persons, things, and actions. Tropology studies how such figures work, and the entry, cross-referring to exegesis, gives readers a compact key to a way of reading that shaped medieval preaching and commentary.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-secular-clerg: Priests who live and work in the wider world, rather than under a religious rule inside a monastery, are known as the secular clergy. This short entry sets them beside the regular clergy. Regular clergy follow a rule and give up personal property. The secular priest keeps his own goods instead. He owes his bishop obedience in church law. He shares the celibacy of ordained life without taking a religious vow.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-slavonic-lang:
Slavonic ranks next to Latin among church languages. Unlike Greek or Latin, which each serve a single rite, it serves both the Greek and Roman rites. In Byzantine form it reaches 115,000,000 people, Catholic and Orthodox, while in Roman form it serves 100,000 Catholics along the Adriatic in Dalmatia and lower Croatia. Cyril and Methodius translated the Byzantine liturgy and offices from Greek into Old Slavonic about 866.

Cyril devised the Cyrillic alphabet for Slavonic sounds as spoken by Bulgars and Moravians. Methodius translated the whole Bible into Slavonic. Summoned to Rome in 868, the brothers won Adrian II's approval for their Slavonic liturgy. An older Glagolitic alphabet, linked by tradition to Jerome, still survives along the Adriatic highlands. A casual hearer could not tell a Slavonic priest from a Latin one except by the language spoken aloud.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sociology:
Sociology's claim to a place among the sciences draws varied dispute, this entry says. Some deny it any distinct problem beyond the accepted social sciences, while others grant its future prospects but fault its present state. Popular confusion worsens matters, mixing sociology with charity, reform, statistics, socialism, sanitation, criminology, and politics. Yet the young science has won university recognition and deeply affected nearby sciences.

Its method is mainly inductive, drawing on ethnology, comparison, statistics, and the study of mind, while its core problem is finding and explaining patterns among social facts. The sociologist seeks a whole view of movements such as democracy, liberty, war, tariffs, labour organization, and class conflict, tracing their wider bearings and place within social processes. Deductive system-building has not yet produced undisputed results.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-teleology:
Teleology, from Greek telos, end, and logos, science, is seldom used for the branch of philosophy dealing with ends or final causes. It usually means the doctrine that design, purpose, or finality exists in the world. Effects are in some manner intentional, and no complete account of the universe is possible without final causes. With mechanism, it admits determined efficient causes and the search for laws.

Against mechanism, it claims that laws and efficient causes reveal a directive principle and finality in nature. The question is not whether man sees because he has eyes or has eyes in order to see. Final and efficient causes are not mutually exclusive. Any result follows an unbroken chain of active causes, and final cause explains how that activity is directed toward useful results. Nor must it name every end, any more than mechanism must name every cause.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-alexandri:
Egypt's ancient pattern of worship takes centre stage here, traced back by tradition to Mark the Evangelist, first bishop of Alexandria. From that parent rite, the entry explains, grew three families still in use across the old patriarchate. They were the Greek Liturgy of Saint Mark, Coptic versions drawn from it, and Ethiopian uses built on the Liturgy of the Twelve Apostles.

By setting these rites side by side, scholars can partly rebuild the worship of Alexandria before the split over Monophysite teaching and the Council of Chalcedon in 451. Early witnesses such as Clement, Athanasius, Serapion, and Pseudo-Dionysius supply further clues. The entry walks through the Mass of the Catechumens and the Mass of the Faithful, from readings and psalms to the kiss of peace and the Eucharistic prayer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-cross-and:
Cross in worship, as object, gesture, feast, and sign, fills this wide liturgical entry under eight heads. Material objects open it. The altar cross is hardly traceable before the thirteenth century, despite Tours's canon of 567, which likely meant Host particles laid crosswise on the corporal, not a cross standing on the altar. Innocent III's treatise on the Mass shows the newer custom.

Liturgical forms, feasts of the Holy Cross, rite of Adoration, manual sign of blessing, church dedications, orders and crusades, and the cross outside Catholicism follow in turn. Processional crosses, pectoral crosses, and blessings with the cross reveal a symbol woven into every hour of Catholic prayer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-law-of-co:
Modern physics meets theism in this long philosophical entry, centred on the Law of Conservation of Energy. Critics have pressed it against miracles, free will, and the soul's immateriality, creation, and immortality, and the entry answers as fully as space allows. Energy, from Greek energeia or operation, means in science the capacity of an agent for doing work.

Work means producing motion against resistance. Energy appears in two states: kinetic, or energy of motion, and potential, or energy of position. From these definitions the entry builds its case, testing whether a fixed total of energy truly shuts out divine action or leaves room for a soul that acts without adding force.
chess-strategy:
Chess Strategy, by Edward Lasker and translated by J du Mont, teaches the game as a contest of plans rather than a hunt for traps. Lasker wrote this second edition text, dated 1915 in its own note, with one hundred sixty seven diagrams of chess and checkers positions. The boards are drawn in plain text characters, with a key explaining the letters used for rook, knight, bishop, queen, king, and pawn.

Two parts organize the teaching, each with its own chapters and prefaces from author and translator. Readers who find the text diagrams hard to read are advised to set positions up on a real board with actual pieces. The approach suits patient students: learn how pieces work together, how pawns shape a position, and how a small edge grows into a win. Lasker, a master player, writes as a teacher first.
civics-as-applied-sociology:
Civics: as Applied Sociology, by Patrick Geddes, argues that the study of cities should be run as a branch of sociology. Geddes praises Charles Booth's social survey of London, yet warns that the vast city makes a poor starting point. A foggy labyrinth, he calls it, from which smaller places show only dimly.

His method begins with the region. A valley read from above shows hunting wastes, pastoral hills, crofts, and hamlets in their order. Below them stand the upland village, the market town at the rail junction, and at last the fisher at sea level. Each place, and each worker in it, is to be traced in turn as a contribution to the whole civic body.
criminal-sociology:
Enrico Ferri, an Italian follower of Cesare Lombroso, set out the new science of criminal sociology in this study of crime and criminals. Ferri argues that crime grows from bodily, mental, and social causes working together. One part surveys criminal anthropology, meaning the study of the criminal's body and mind, from skulls and faces to heredity and moral feeling.

Later parts sort criminals into classes: born criminals, habitual criminals, occasional criminals, criminals of passion, and the insane. Statistics on crime rates support the scheme. Ferri wanted punishment fitted to the type of offender, with prevention ranked above revenge. Modern readers will find some claims dated, but the book shaped how Europe debated crime.
doe-osti-2583365-shaping-symmetry-and-mo:
Award DE-SC0022067's closing report, from Edwin L. Thomas at Texas A&M and covering September 2021 to March 2025, chases designer nanostructures in block copolymers. These plastics self-assemble into triply periodic networks, lattices threading through space in three directions. The double gyroid is the famous member; the team wanted the rest of the family, whose connected channels suit photonics, supercapacitors, and ultrafiltration membranes.

The headline result is a way to measure packing frustration, the cost when chains stretch to fill a complex shape. The team defined a medial thickness, read off the surface between the two polymer domains. Field theory confirmed that chains really do follow the medial map. Slice-and-view electron microscopy rebuilt domains in 3D so the measure could be tested on experiments. Theory came from Grason's group and synthesis from Coughlin's. Twelve papers, one more in review, and two dissertations came out of the award.
doe-osti-2583504-testing-and-expertise-f:
CRADA final report NREL/TP-5000-94901, dated May 6, 2024, puts rotating seals for ocean energy devices on a life-test rig. Robynne Murray was NREL's contact under the TEAMER support program. Dynamic seals keep seawater out of the moving shafts in wave and tidal converters, and they must do it for years underwater with no maintenance visits. The marine energy industry, unlike older marine industries, had almost no performance data for them.

NREL used and augmented a custom special-purpose test system to run accelerated-life testing on candidate seals and seal arrangements. The aim was a rigorous testing framework: which factors govern seal life, and how should the industry measure them? Results feed directly into standards development for this critical component. A seal failure at sea is not a warranty claim; it can end a device. The project treats an unglamorous rubber ring with the seriousness its consequences deserve.
doe-osti-2589118-glass-furnace-decarboni:
Owens-Brockway Glass Container Incorporated, part of O-I Glass, filed this final technical report for award DE-CD0000093 from the Office of Clean Energy Demonstrations, submitted September 22, 2025. John Jenkinson was principal investigator. The catalog record names no author; the report is the company's own account of its Glass Furnace Decarbonization Technology Stack.

Glass container furnaces run hot around the clock, and their fuel burn is the industry's carbon problem. The project's goal, as its objectives list puts it, is to install the furnace technology stack and commence commercial operations producing commercial quality soda-lime glass containers. In other words, decarbonization proven at production scale, not in a pilot. The report also carries community commitments. It pledges better air quality for nearby communities. It pledges engagement with workers toward project labor agreements and workforce pacts, with workers' rights and equity named outright.
doe-osti-3005418-siting-prioritization-f:
Gale Hauck, Hope Corsair, Niki Luke, and David Pointer of Oak Ridge propose a fairer map for reactor siting in report ORNL/SPR-2025/4339, dated November 2025. New nuclear plants need sites, and siting history carries real grievances. The team builds an energy justice framework into the prioritization itself, rather than consulting communities after the map is drawn.

The report reviews how justice has been handled in energy system optimization models and in geographic siting frameworks for other technologies. Economic evaluation tools for Generation IV reactors appear among the building blocks. The aim is a screening process that weighs burden and benefit distribution alongside geology and grid access. For an industry asking towns to host reactors again, the order of those questions matters, and this framework puts them up front.
doe-osti-3006042-center-for-wind-energy:
Final technical report DE-EE0010673 from the University of Texas at Dallas, submitted October 30, 2025, documents the stand-up of a Center for Wind Energy on the Richardson campus. Mario Rotea directed the center. The award bought physical infrastructure and added measurement equipment for wind energy research, education, technology development, and community outreach, with university, civic, and industry partners involved. The project period ran from November 1, 2023 to April 30, 2025.

The report is candid about friction: supply chain problems, worse than expected at the start, delayed several equipment deliveries despite eager vendors and fast purchase orders. Naming faculty custodians for each piece of equipment helped push purchases through. Those custodians are also expected to maintain the equipment in service. The center's purpose is to create and test new wind technologies with its partners.
doe-osti-3008999-final-report-for-theore:
Final technical report for DOE grant DE-SC0020220, by Chanda Prescod-Weinstein of the University of New Hampshire, closes six years of theoretical high energy physics support, June 2019 to May 2025. The award backed three faculty: Prescod-Weinstein, Per Berglund, and David Mattingly.

Prescod-Weinstein's thread followed axion-like dark matter. Her PhD student Anthony Mirasola defended his dissertation in spring 2025 on four co-authored papers. Those papers examine how self-interactions, black holes, and multi-field setups shape dark matter halos. Mattingly's group pursued quantum gravity phenomenology and black hole thermodynamics. Berglund worked with students on machine learning for the geometry of Calabi-Yau manifolds in string theory.
doe-osti-3013637-new-engineering-concept:
Prashant Kumta of the University of Pittsburgh led this final report on new engineering concepts for high-energy-density lithium-sulfur batteries, running October 2021 to June 2025 with 1.54 million dollars in funding. Lithium-sulfur cells promise energy density above 500 watt-hours per kilogram, but sulfur's discharge products dissolve and migrate to the anode, killing cycle life, and lithium dendrites add a safety hazard.

The team attacked on three fronts: confinement cathodes that trap sulfur, electrocatalysts that speed full conversion of polysulfides, and lithium alloy anodes found by theory. One cathode design using an FEC additive opened near 900 milliamp-hours per gram at slow rates and still held 520 after 150 cycles at about 98 percent coulombic efficiency. The results map what a commercial lithium-sulfur cell still needs.
doe-osti-3014925-testing-and-expertise-f:
CRADA final report CRD-20-17302, dated January 2026, records support for the Testing and Expertise for Marine Energy program. The program is known as TEAMER. The National Laboratory of the Rockies issued the report. TEAMER routes marine energy developers to test facilities and experts across a national network. The laboratory's contacts coordinated that support. Fredrick Driscoll was a lab technical contact.

The report documents the assistance structure behind the program. Developers bring wave, tidal, and current energy devices or components. The network matches them with tank tests and flume runs. It also matches them with modeling help and field expertise. Alone, they could not easily reach those resources. Work of this kind shortens the path from prototype to open-water trial. That is where marine energy designs meet real loads and real failure modes for the first time.
doe-osti-3015312-development-of-wireless:
A GuRu Wireless SBIR Phase I final report under award DE-SC0025099, dated March 28, 2025, aims to power smart windows without wires. Electrochromic windows change tint on electrical command. Retrofit installs, though, often stall on the cost of running power to each pane. The project adapted GuRu's RF lensing wireless power system to feed window controllers. Behrooz Abiri was principal investigator.

Testing used the Advanced Windows Testbed at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. One controller there manages tint for windows in adjoining rooms. A site visit changed the design. The controller has a single power input. Half a room could not be split off as planned. The wireless system thus had to scale up to power the whole controller load. The report closes with conclusions, recommendations, and lessons learned from that rescope.
doe-osti-3018127-design-status-and-exper:
Kenneth Cooper, Anthony Birri, and Richard Howard of Oak Ridge National Laboratory, with Rishi Pillai and Heath McCartney, wrote this February 2026 report, ORNL/SPR-2026/4390. It sets the design status and experimental strategy for the first molten salt irradiation experiments in HFIR, the High Flux Isotope Reactor. Molten salt reactors cannot be qualified on modeling alone: someone must irradiate real salt and real structural metal together.

The gap is specific. Separate tests miss the coupled effects of neutron irradiation, temperature, salt chemistry, and time acting at once. The strategy phases upward in complexity: passive, non-fueled static capsules first, then fueled and instrumented capsules, and ultimately circulating salt loops. A Phase 1 passive capsule concept is defined, with its irradiation conditions and a post-irradiation examination plan. Supporting modeling, bench testing, and safety analysis are described. Reactor developers get the on-ramp plan for the data their licenses will require.
doe-osti-3366886-launch-alaska-transport:
Launch Alaska's final report for DOE EPIC award DE-EE0009608 closes the Launch Alaska Transportation and Energy Accelerator. Timothy Leach submitted it, with Isaac Vanderburg as project lead. The accelerator ran October 2021 to June 2025. It recruited transportation startups and tested their products in Alaska, where extreme cold, scattered communities, and the nation's highest energy costs expose weaknesses hidden in milder markets.

Results exceeded most objectives: 42 companies recruited, 23 accepted into cohorts, seven proof-of-concept projects, and 25 transportation projects accelerated, representing about 605.9 million dollars. Electric vehicle demos in harsh conditions anchored the outreach. An Electrified Alaska film kept shaping fleet decisions after the grant. Partner withdrawals mid-project forced replans the report recounts. Alaska-proven technology, the argument goes, transfers to rural and Arctic users everywhere.
doe-osti-3375764-advanced-mooring-lines-:
SAND2026-22669, a Sandia National Laboratories report printed in June 2026, sums up a workshop on advanced mooring lines for marine energy. Eight authors compiled it, led by Peter J. Creveling, Bernadette A. Hernandez-Sanchez, and Budi Gunawan. Mooring lines hold wave and tidal power rigs in place at sea. A line that parts can wreck a device and end a project. The field is shifting from steel chain and wire toward synthetic rope, whose long-term behavior at sea is less well known.

Sessions covered line materials past and future. Other blocks took up failure modes, sea-driven wear, and health monitoring. Test sites, measurement skill, and standards got their own round. Polls put hard questions to the room. On model skill, the group agreed on a gap: today's tools do not call synthetic line life with care. Time-linked wear across scales is a named weak spot.
doe-osti-3422014-hydrodynamic-modelling-:
In August 2026, the National Laboratory of the Rockies released report NLR/TP-5700-100873, which models water flow around tidal energy kites. Thanh Toan Tran was the lab contact. The work ran under CRADA number CRD-24-30123. A kite turbine, named the Manta Kite system in the text, flies through tidal currents to make power.

One task built a two-phase, three-dimensional fluid model from partner data. The model used the partner's design drawing as its shape base. Uncertainty checks covered grid spacing and time step size. Tidal developers need trusted flow models before towing costly prototypes to sea.
govdocs-archive_org-nciplesOfTopological:
Kurt Lewin, the Gestalt psychologist who founded much of modern social psychology, published Principles of Topological Psychology with McGraw-Hill in 1936. The book sets out his field theory, the idea that behavior is a function of the person and their environment taken together.

Lewin maps what he calls the life space, the whole situation as a person experiences it, using ideas from topology to draw its regions, paths, and barriers. The method was his attempt to give psychology scientific rigor without losing the wholeness Gestalt theory prized. The book remains a landmark of social psychology.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_nuclear-:
The International Atomic Energy Agency, the world's nuclear watchdog, came into existence in 1956 and 1957. William Burr edited this briefing book, posted in October 2017 for its sixtieth anniversary. The agency was born despite complete skepticism from the Soviet Union.

India and other countries fought sharply over whether inspections would be equitable. The United States insisted that an American head the new organization. Those founding arguments, over fairness and control, still shape the agency's work. The documents show an institution designed amid distrust, which may explain why its inspection system was built to survive disagreement rather than assume goodwill.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_cyber-vault_Repor: The Office of Technology Assessment was Congress's own science adviser from 1972 until lawmakers abolished it in 1995, producing hundreds of studies on everything from missile defense to medical care. A National Security Archive posting presents reports from that office as part of its Cyber Vault collection, preserving the work of an institution the government itself discarded. OTA reports were prized for plain language and honest weighing of options. They serve readers who want careful assessments of technology questions, written for legislators rather than specialists or salesmen.
homer-and-classical-philology:
Friedrich Nietzsche gave this address at Bâle University on the twenty-eighth of May 1869. It was his inaugural lecture as a young professor. The hosted text comes from the third volume of his complete works in English, issued in 1910. Nietzsche asks what classical philology truly is.

No clear view of the science is held, he argues, even by its own followers. Philology borrows from many sciences and mixes them like a magic potion. On Homer, he treats the name as a material category before it was a man's. The contest with Hesiod shows no sense of the single author, he holds. Readers meet Nietzsche the scholar before Nietzsche the prophet.
music-notation-and-terminology:
Karl W. Gehrkens of Oberlin Conservatory wrote this guide to written music. The A. S. Barnes Company issued it in New York in 1914. Chapter one lays out rules for correct notation. It covers notes, stems, cross-strokes, and rests.

Gehrkens wrote for school music teachers and their classes. Terms are defined in plain order, with figures to show each point. The text even thanks helpers for a figured bass example. An audio-linked HTML version pairs terms with sound. The book served as a standard class text, a dictionary and rulebook for how music should look on the page.
nasa-tm-19690008664-photodisintegration-:
F. W. Stecker, of the Theoretical Studies Branch at Goddard Space Flight Center, wrote this December 1968 preprint, X-641-68-480. He studies photodisintegration: atomic nuclei flying at ultrahigh energy, broken apart by light that fills all of space. Such cosmic ray nuclei cross vast distances before reaching Earth, and the universal radiation field attacks them the whole way.

Stecker calculates in detail how effective that breakup process really is. He concludes it cannot explain the air shower observations at the highest energies by itself. One escape remains, he notes: a large flow of infrared light between the galaxies, which may recently have been detected. The paper closes by discussing what else its results imply for cosmic ray origins.
nasa-tm-19710007275-calibration-of-the-n:
H. Whiteside of Federal City College and C. J. Crannell and H. Crannell of Catholic University joined J. F. Ormes and M. J. Ryan of Goddard on this report. It is a preliminary report, dated January 1971. It covers the calibration of Goddard's high energy cosmic ray experiment.

The instrument was checked against a test beam at Brookhaven National Laboratory. The report describes the conditions under which that calibration ran. It gives a detailed account of the test beam's momentum. Summaries of the data runs taken are also included. A detector must be calibrated on known beams before its space readings can be trusted.
nasa-tm-19710008961-space-shuttle-avioni: Space Shuttle Avionics Technology is the title of a NASA technical memorandum on the electronic control and guidance systems planned for the space shuttle. Avionics covers the computers, sensors, and wiring that let a crew fly and manage the vehicle. The hosted sample preserves only a reproduction notice and garbled scan pages. No author, center, date, or readable abstract survives in the sample. The report's specific systems and findings therefore cannot be described from the evidence provided here.
nasa-tm-19720016318-useful-new-technolog:
Useful New Technology is a NASA booklet explaining the Technology Utilization Program. Space research produced far more than rockets and moonshots. New materials, tools, and methods spilled into ordinary life. The program existed to spread those advances widely. Its stated aim was a better return on the public's space investment. Industry, schools, hospitals, and cities were all invited to draw on the results. The booklet tells readers how to take part.

Chapters cover the industrial benefits already gained from space work. They explain how to obtain NASA technical data for a problem. Special publications and regional dissemination centers are described. Multidisciplinary application teams match space solutions to outside needs. Interagency work, patents, and licenses close the survey. A closing chapter looks at what the future might hold.
nassau-bantu-sociology:
Robert Hamill Nassau distilled forty years in Gabon into Bantu Sociology in 1914. The missionary knew West African life from the inside, not from books. Kinship, law, marriage, and custom stand as his main subjects here.

Nassau shows how clan ties order birth, work, worship, and death. He treats Bantu custom as a full system, worthy of respect. His long residence gives each rule a human face and story. The book pairs with his Fetichism in West Africa in the catalog. Missionary records at their most humane and detailed fill these careful pages. Nassau judges custom by its inner logic, not by foreign scorn.
on-the-study-of-zoology:
Thomas Henry Huxley wrote this lecture on studying zoology. He begins with the old, wide sense of natural history. Linnaeus covered minerals, plants, and animals in one system. No single scholar could repeat that feat now, Huxley says. Knowledge has grown too vast for one mind.

Zoology and botany have grown closer together, he argues. Both now sit under the common head of biology. Mineralogy has drifted away from its old partners. Students must choose animals or plants and specialize. Broad laws still link the living kingdoms, he notes. Huxley urges learning from living animals directly.
podcast-dannyjones-JnKYgCrarGY:
Jaime Rogozinski, founder of the WallStreetBets forum, joins Danny Jones to explain his creation. He started the forum in 2012 as a small online group. It grew into a force that shook big funds.

Rogozinski says he never expected crowds of small traders to move prices so far. He wrote a book on how older wealth built a casino for the young. Jones asks about greed, rules, and outright corruption. The episode traces how a joke-heavy forum became a real power in modern markets. The story now reads like modern market history.
podcast-joerogan-k2D-xNI7XgY:
Comedian Luis J. Gomez returns to Joe Rogan for episode 2486. Gomez co-hosts the brash show Legion of Skanks. His style is loud, fast, and proudly crude.

Rogan and Gomez trade tales from New York's raw comedy scene. They discuss podcast wars, roasts, and loyalty among comics. Gomez defends his crew and their no-rules format. The episode is a rowdy hang between regulars. Fans of the Skanks world get their man on the biggest stage, sounding exactly like himself at every turn. Raw rooms made both men who they are.
select-epigrams-from-the-greek-anthology: J. W. Mackail stands as the maker of a choice of short poems drawn from the Greek Anthology, in English form. The pages at hand carry only the publisher's header for the electronic edition, with the title and Mackail's name. No epigram text, opening notes, or list of contents appears in these first pages. Which poets and themes Mackail chose, and how he rendered them, cannot be stated fairly from the header alone.
siouan-sociology:
James Owen Dorsey wrote this study of Siouan social life, issued after his death in the Bureau of Ethnology's fifteenth annual report, printed at Washington in 1897. Dorsey went to Dakota Territory in 1871, aged twenty-three, as a missionary among the Ponka Indians. Amiability and a rare ear for speech won him trust fast.

Two years among the Ponka grounded Dorsey in their tongue and kindred dialects. He gathered rich stores on arts, customs, traditions, and beliefs. Illness drove him home in 1873, yet study went on. His record preserves how Siouan peoples ordered kin, camp, and ceremony.
some-principles-of-maritime-strategy: Julian S. Corbett sets out Some Principles of Maritime Strategy, printed at London in 1911. The contents divide the book into a study of war in the abstract, a theory of naval war, and the conduct of naval war. Early heads sort wars as attack or defense, and as limited or without limit, with a part on limited war and sea empires. Sea command forms the core of the naval theory.
the-broadway-anthology: The Broadway Anthology was made by Edward L. Bernays, Samuel Hoffenstein, Walter J. Kingsley, and Murdock Pemberton. Duffield and Company of New York put it out, with rights dated 1917. A note of thanks names the New York Evening Post, Sun, Times, and Tribune, the Boston Transcript, and the Wilmarth Publishing Company, for leave to reprint matter. Bernays' pieces come first in the list. They are Accidents Will Happen, The Baritone, Patriotism, and The Pillow Cases. Hoffenstein's The Theatre Scrubwoman Dreams a Dream starts the next name's work.
the-elements-of-geology: The Elements of Geology, by William Harmon Norton, is the work named across the old Project Gutenberg header pages at the front of this text. Those pages give the title and the author's full name. They also note a July 2003 release for the e-text. Only the header matter is present here. None of Norton's chapters appear, so nothing of his treatment of rocks and deep time can be drawn from what is shown.
the-entire-march-family-trilogy:
William Dean Howells's March Family Trilogy binds three Basil March books in one: Their Wedding Journey, A Hazard of New Fortunes, and Their Silver Wedding Journey. The first, dated 1871, tells how Basil and Isabel met in Boston. They matched in Europe, then broke off. Years later they matched again. The narrator owns he cannot rehearse their long love tale in full.

Niagara and the St. Lawrence fill the honeymoon book. The middle novel turns to New York magazine life and labour strife. Howells, dean of American realism, tracks one marriage across a changing nation.
the-harvard-classics-volume-38-scientifi:
The Harvard Classics Volume 38 gathers scientific papers. The subjects are physiology, medicine, surgery, and geology. The contents list the Oath and the Law of Hippocrates. Journeys by Ambroise Pare appear in a translation by Stephen Paget. William Harvey on the motion of the heart and blood appears in a translation by Robert Willis. Edward Jenner on vaccination against smallpox is also listed.

Later pieces include O. W. Holmes on puerperal fever. Lord Lister writes on the antiseptic principle in surgery. Louis Pasteur writes on fermentation and the germ theory. Sir Charles Lyell writes on claims that held back geology. An opening note begins with Hippocrates, the Greek physician born on Cos.
the-haunted-hour-an-anthology: Margaret Widdemer compiled The Haunted Hour, an anthology. Harcourt, Brace and Howe published it in New York in 1920. Long copyright notices stand before the text. The notices credit the holders of the poems included. Names include Joyce Kilmer and May Byron. Rudyard Kipling is credited for The Looking-Glass. Other names include Arthur Guiterman and Don Marquis. Amy Lowell is also credited. Only the title page and copyright notices are present here. The poems themselves do not appear.
the-student-s-elements-of-geology: Sir Charles Lyell prepared this student's textbook. He also wrote The Principles of Geology and The Antiquity of Man. The book holds more than six hundred illustrations on wood. Harper and Brothers published it in New York in 1878. Only the title page and a detailed contents opening appear here. The contents sum up chapters. They treat the classes of rocks. They treat how aqueous rocks are composed and layered. They treat the arrangement of fossils in fresh-water and sea beds. Lyell's lessons themselves do not appear.
town-geology:
Paper one of this geology series treats the soil of the field, after a general introduction to the science. Geology, the writer says, explains only the rind of the earth, not its mass, which belongs to astronomy. A fruit comparison makes the point: astronomy studies the whole fruit, geology its covering.

That rind's beauty and complexity still merit reverent study, telling of mountain ranges, continents, and whole worlds of plants and animals rising and decaying. Geology also trains sound scientific habits without mathematics or obscure Latin. No author is named in what is present. Readers get popular science written for ordinary observers.
